record.title: Response to two differently connected duct openings
fairness: One defensible immediate plan among the offered choices is subhepatic drainage and hepatobiliary-center transfer. The reader must combine the distal injection reaching the duodenum with the separate upper injection filling both hepatic ducts, then apply the continuity finding and the local expertise limit. Routine transpapillary diversion does not solve the described separation.

The record supplies more than contrast escaping around a catheter: it describes a distal segment emptying from its upper end, two visible open ends and complementary proximal/distal filling. The explanation correctly cautions that reflux around an injection site alone would not establish this injury. No exact injury grade, repair timing or reconstruction method is demanded without adequate information.

The third option represents extending local dissection to define the proximal injury before handoff. It is less appropriate with drainage already feasible and reconstruction outside the surgeon's practice. This is a recognizable staging-versus-preservation error, although it is weaker than the communicating-leak/stent distractor; difficulty is moderate rather than hard.

Cue attack: 'The operating surgeon does not perform biliary reconstruction' is a legitimate decision-critical constraint, not a direct lexical match to a unique option. Both transfer and requested stenting involve outside expertise, so the learner still has to interpret continuity. All choices share drainage; the key is not uniquely comprehensive, longest or qualified by a rationale. No diagnosis label explicitly names complete transection before the choice.

The sequence is interpretable without inventing an intervening duct division: the first presentation says the presumed cystic duct has not been divided; the second record describes additional main-duct ends connected to different systems. Discovery of an unrecognized injury is plausible. The second injection is through an already exposed end, so the text does not require the very proximal dissection offered as a distractor.

The second node stands with its shared patient presentation, current update and constructed injection record. It does not depend on remembering the first key. The first explanation primes attention to continuity but does not supply this finding or management answer. The exhibit adds discriminating evidence for rejecting ordinary stenting rather than merely repeating the prior unexplained-bile observation.

The live ASC setting remains plausible for recognition and immediate control of an unexpected injury, with definitive specialist care elsewhere. The item does not portray major biliary reconstruction as an ambulatory-center operation. Stability, available exposure and the expertise boundary are present. This is high-yield bile-duct injury management.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the visible text. Exact injection interpretation and management claims remain subject to named clinical review; this offline editorial PASS does not verify sources or confer clinical approval.
suggestions: Optional chronology polish: introduce the table as the completed two-injection sequence, explicitly placing exposure of the upper end before its injection and final catheter removal after acquisition. The current record is understandable, but a brief temporal bridge would reduce rereading.
Retain the separate injection origins, visible open ends and both filling distributions. Do not simplify them to 'contrast extravasates' or replace them with an injury diagnosis.

Keep both the expertise limit and adequate drainage exposure. Do not manufacture difficulty by withholding facts that establish why transfer rather than local reconstruction or exposure for immediate control is appropriate.

record.title: Immediate plan after a main-duct gap is mapped
clarityIssues: The sequence starts with identified cystic structures awaiting division and an unlocalized stream, then jumps to two exposed open duct ends with an intervening segment absent. 'The surgeon has now obtained the duct studies shown below' does not explain how these ends became visible or how tissue loss was established. A resident may wonder whether the injury was discovered during mapping or caused by an omitted intervening maneuver. This is a chronology gap, not a claim that such an injury is anatomically impossible.

The first injection says the opacified channel 'ends proximally in the operative field'. State the observed contrast behavior at that end if it is part of the inference; an abrupt radiographic endpoint by itself could describe an obstruction rather than an open end. The separate operative-field row currently supplies the missing interpretation.

The task is complete, and the local update/exhibit make the management question solvable even without the first answer. The stable anesthetic status and operator experience are relevant. The construction label is honest; no actual cholangiogram image is promised.

cues.phrase: does not perform biliary reconstruction
cues.why: This explicitly removes both operative reconstruction choices before the learner interprets the duct studies. The constraint is legitimate and must remain, but two of four options are consequently weak competitors in this ASC scene. Strengthen the choices rather than hide the lack of expertise. This cue does not by itself distinguish referral from the remaining stenting plan.

fairness: The supplied combination of distal duct/duodenal filling, separately demonstrated proximal hepatic ducts and an actual tissue gap supports major loss of continuity. Applying that to the limits of routine transpapillary diversion, then selecting contamination control and specialist care when reconstruction expertise is absent, gives two consequential steps. The meaningful remaining error is treating this as a communicating minor leak.

Drainage and transfer is the defensible best answer in the stated setting. The explanation appropriately leaves definitive reconstruction method and timing to specialist assessment rather than asserting that one timing rule applies universally. No confident clinical inaccuracy in that management conclusion is identified in this offline review.

A serious injury arising during an otherwise appropriate ASC procedure is a plausible live complication. Recognizing it and arranging transfer belongs in the ASC encounter; actually performing major biliary reconstruction there would not fit the stated setting. The hospital-level distractors should not be mistaken for authorization to enact those procedures locally.

The displayed gap is sufficient to make routine papillary stenting unattractive even if the two injection rows are removed. Thus the table contains useful anatomical documentation, but its full interpretation is not currently necessary to solve the item. This limits difficulty; it does not make the answer unfair.

The earlier explanation teaches mapping before treatment but does not disclose drainage/transfer or the continuity-versus-stenting boundary. There is no decisive preceding-feedback leak. The follow-up is independently answerable once its current observations are accepted, while the physical transition from the preceding checkpoint still needs repair.
The precise acquisition sequence and the certainty of tissue loss should be confirmed by the clinical sign-off. No unseen maneuver, injury mechanism or newly verified evidence is assumed here.
suggestions: Add a short, clinically reviewed transition explaining discovery of the existing injury and the origin of each injection. State what was observed after suction/exposure, without implying that additional hazardous dissection or removal of duct was necessary merely to demonstrate it.

Make the contrast descriptions precise enough to distinguish extravasation/open discontinuity from nonfilling or obstruction. Do not add an unsupported measurement or injury classification just to increase apparent sophistication.

Retain the operator-expertise and stability information. Replace at least one locally unavailable reconstruction distractor with a plausible immediate management plan that remains a real choice in this setting, and verify the new ranking with the clinician.

Decide whether this node primarily tests map interpretation or response to an already established tissue-loss injury. If interpretation is the objective, make the relationship between the injection findings necessary; if management is the objective, shorten redundant mapping detail. Preserve the independent continuity-versus-stenting decision.

record.title: Immediate plan after main-duct discontinuity is documented
clarityIssues: 'Perform open surgical injury staging' is not a sufficiently concrete operative plan. A resident must infer whether this means conversion for inspection, further hilar dissection, vascular assessment or a reconstructive attempt. The explanation supplies a narrower diagnostic-exploration meaning than the option itself states.

The distal and proximal injection origins are now understandable, and the exhibit supplies the relationship of the hepatic system to the distal duct and duodenum. 'Contrast spills from the injected end' can also describe reflux around a catheter; the already visible separate open ends supply the discontinuity evidence. The explanation should not imply that injection-site escape alone proves transection.

The shared 'identified before division' presentation still leaves the earlier operative sequence uncertain. The current update clearly says the ends were exposed by suction/retraction and were not created during this assessment; keep that distinction while clarifying the earlier checkpoint.

cues.phrase: The operating surgeon does not perform biliary reconstruction.
cues.why: This is a legitimate management constraint, but it directly favors the only explicit specialist-transfer plan. Neither distractor is itself reconstruction, so it does not mechanically exclude them; nevertheless, with two visible open ends it makes the map less necessary for a test-wise transfer choice. Retain the constraint, but strengthen the competing management decision.

cues.phrase: No intervening duct is divided or excised during this assessment.
cues.why: This defensive negative emphasizes restraint immediately before an option to 'perform open surgical injury staging.' It is useful chronology, not an absolute prohibition, but can function as a pre-answer warning against further exploration. Express discovery as a positive sequence of observed actions where possible.

fairness: Drainage and hepatobiliary-center transfer is the best offered immediate plan. Separate proximal hepatic and distal duodenal systems explain why the ordinary communicating-leak transpapillary-stent pathway is inadequate. No confident clinical error in that central ranking was identified.

Two consequential steps remain: use the acquisitions to establish which duct systems are disconnected, then apply that relationship and the local expertise limit to select immediate contamination control and specialist care. This is moderate management reasoning, not hard image interpretation; the description of two open ends and the expertise sentence substantially lower difficulty.

Routine transpapillary stenting is a credible misconception for a resident familiar with postoperative leaks. The explanation appropriately says 'Routine' and does not claim that every specialist endoscopic, percutaneous or combined technique is impossible.

The vague open-staging alternative weakens fairness and discrimination. The supplied stable circulation and successful laparoscopic acquisitions make additional diagnostic exploration less compelling, but they do not justify an unrestricted rule against conversion for exposure or control. The explanation correctly preserves that distinction; the option should state the actual proposed action.

The two acquisitions are anatomically intelligible if the cystic duct joins the distal segment below the demonstrated interruption. Exact safe catheter manipulation and interpretation require clinician confirmation; no new injury level, vascular injury, reconstruction timing or repair technique can be inferred from this record.

Recognition, contamination control and transfer for an unexpected complication during adult ASC cholecystectomy are plausible. This does not authorize definitive hospital-level reconstruction or live ERCP in the clinic. The scene remains consistent with the program's setting boundary.

The first node's explanation does not rehearse transfer or the stenting limitation. Discovery followed by separate acquisitions and then a management choice is coherent. record.title: Response to two differently connected duct openings
fairness: One defensible immediate plan among the offered choices is subhepatic drainage and hepatobiliary-center transfer. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Cholangiography fills both hepatic ducts and the duodenum and shows a persistent distal common-duct stone on repeat views after flushing. The common duct measures 5 mm. A guidewire passes through the short angulated cystic duct, but the smallest available extraction basket cannot follow it; the cystic-duct wall begins to split at the opening with gentle instrument passage. Circulation remains stable.
decisionNodes.stem: Which completion and duct-clearance plan best fits {patientName}'s findings during laparoscopic cholecystectomy?

answerChoices.label: Complete cholecystectomy and arrange retrograde transpapillary stone extraction
answerChoices.rationale: Further transcystic passage is limited by the splitting narrow route. Direct common-duct incision carries an unfavorable caliber here. Complete the gallbladder operation with secure cystic closure and arrange endoscopic stone clearance rather than persisting with either operative route.

answerChoices.label: Complete cholecystectomy after further transcystic dilation and stone extraction
answerChoices.rationale: Extending a small ductotomy or dilating the cystic route can enable clearance in suitable tissue. The current limiting finding is a wall that is already splitting during gentle passage, rather than a small opening in a sound duct.

answerChoices.label: Complete cholecystectomy and arrange stone extraction through a common-duct incision
answerChoices.rationale: A transductal approach can clear stones when transcystic access fails. The narrow common duct makes incision and closure less attractive because of postoperative stricture risk; available expertise does not remove this anatomical constraint.

decisionNodes.explanation: The confirmed stone needs clearance. A splitting cystic duct weighs against further transcystic instrumentation, while the 5-mm common duct weighs against choledochotomy. The SAGES review describes transductal exploration in ducts at least 7 mm wide to limit stricture risk, a selection consideration rather than a biological cliff. With ordinary endoscopic access available, secure the cystic duct, complete cholecystectomy and arrange hospital ERCP. Different duct anatomy or failed endoscopic access could change that ranking.

record.title: Clearance route after a difficult transcystic attempt
fairness: The best offered plan is completion with subsequent endoscopic transpapillary stone extraction. The learner must recognize that successful guidewire passage does not make continued basket passage/dilation appropriate when the cystic-duct wall is splitting, then use common-duct caliber to compare transductal exploration with endoscopic clearance. These are two consequential route-selection judgments.

The closest competitors are credible: further transcystic enlargement can be appropriate in suitable tissue, and transductal exploration can follow failed transcystic access in suitable anatomy. The supplied wall behavior and 5-mm common duct distinguish this case. Removing the tissue finding makes further transcystic work more competitive; removing the caliber leaves the surgical-clearance comparison less well resolved. The findings earn their place.

Calling the persistent finding a stone is acceptable here because the objective is clearance-route selection, not diagnosis from a cholangiogram. Repeated views after flushing, proximal filling and duodenal filling establish the stated procedural checkpoint without requiring an unavailable image to solve an image-recognition task.

Cue attack: all three labels specify completion and a clearance route with comparable length and specificity. None contains an explanatory error, absolute or generic individualized plan. Referral access is stated for both endoscopic and surgical clearance; it does not uniquely authorize the key. Lack of prior gastric/duodenal surgery supplies a relevant conventional-access boundary rather than a diagnosis giveaway.

Live cholecystectomy with an attempted transcystic maneuver is plausible in an appropriately equipped ASC; the presentation explicitly establishes that the team performs this procedure. The keyed ERCP is arranged subsequently, and the explanation locates it at a hospital. The item does not require an ASC to perform choledochotomy or major duct reconstruction. It also does not state that the patient should be discharged home before duct clearance.

The observed splitting needs safe cystic-duct control before completion; the explanation includes securing the duct. No extension into the common duct, uncontrolled bile leak or instability is supplied, so these should not be invented to defeat the offered key. If the intended case includes inability to secure the stump, the completion plan would require reassessment and that finding must be stated.

The 7-mm recommendation appears only in post-answer teaching and is described as a selection consideration, not an absolute biological cutoff. I cannot independently verify its exact SAGES attribution or currency within this offline visible-text review. No replacement threshold is proposed and no confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted. Editorial PASS does not verify that source claim or confer clinical approval.

The adult patient, procedural stage and standalone task are coherent. Choledocholithiasis clearance after failed transcystic access is high yield. Difficulty is moderate because the two anatomical constraints clearly favor one route; this is not a hard item merely because several procedures are named.
suggestions: Optional wording polish: use 'operating team' rather than 'source team' and name 'postoperative hospital ERCP with stone extraction' directly rather than relying on the longer route description. Preserve parallel specificity across options.
Keep the splitting wall and measured common-duct caliber; do not substitute a preinterpreted statement that operative clearance is unsuitable.

Before clinical approval, confirm the exact source support and limitations for the numerical transductal-selection teaching point. Preserve the explanation's qualification and do not turn the cited value into an absolute contraindication.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Irrigation clears the field, but green fluid collects again medial to the gallbladder neck, away from the small duct opening. The gallbladder wall is unbroken. The duct opening is visible, accepts a fine catheter without traction and remains accessible below the gallbladder-side clip.
decisionNodes.stem: Which mapping approach should be used for {patientName}'s recurrent bile at this laparoscopic cholecystectomy checkpoint?

answerChoices.label: Acquire a transcystic contrast cholangiogram using fluoroscopy
answerChoices.rationale: The accessible opening is below the clip and permits contrast to enter the ductal tree. Recurrent bile outside the unbroken gallbladder calls for assessment of the lumen and any escape of contrast.

answerChoices.label: Acquire a gallbladder-injection contrast cholangiogram using fluoroscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Gallbladder injection is an operative cholangiography route when it communicates with the ducts. At this checkpoint the clip closes that outlet; filling the gallbladder would not provide the intended ductal study.

answerChoices.label: Acquire a fluorescence cholangiogram using near-infrared imaging
answerChoices.rationale: Fluorescence is useful for anatomical orientation, and ICG is already available in the bile. It does not replace the selected contrast study of the ductal lumen and extravasation in this new-bile assessment. The guideline preference is conditional, not a universal prohibition on fluorescence.

decisionNodes.explanation: Recurrent bile outside an unbroken gallbladder changes the imaging objective from orientation to assessment of a possible duct leak. Contrast can enter the ducts through the accessible opening below the clip; injection into the gallbladder would encounter the closed outlet. Fluorescence remains a useful adjunct, but the proposed contrast study defines luminal continuity and contrast escape. This checkpoint does not establish an injury class or its treatment.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At the next checkpoint, the catheter has been removed. Suction and gentle retraction bring two open duct ends into view within the existing dissection field. Circulation remains stable and laparoscopic exposure permits drainage. The operating surgeon does not perform biliary reconstruction. The acquisition record is shown below.
decisionNodes.stem: Which immediate plan should be selected for {patientName} after these findings during laparoscopic cholecystectomy?

answerChoices.label: Drain the subhepatic space and arrange hepatobiliary-center transfer
answerChoices.rationale: These acquisitions connect the intrahepatic system and papilla to different open ends in the field. With bile control achievable and no local reconstructive expertise, drainage and hepatobiliary-center transfer provide the appropriate immediate bridge to specialist treatment.

answerChoices.label: Drain the subhepatic space and request transpapillary stenting
answerChoices.rationale: A routine transpapillary stent diverts a communicating leak through the distal outlet. Here the upper study fills both hepatic ducts without reaching that outlet, while the lower study reaches the duodenum without filling the hepatic system. Ordinary stenting alone does not reconnect them; specialist combined techniques are a separate question.

answerChoices.label: Drain the subhepatic space and dissect proximally to expose the hepatic confluence
answerChoices.rationale: The complementary studies already show the hepatic system and distal outlet opening separately. Further proximal dissection for a more complete injury description can compromise tissue needed by the receiving specialist. This differs from gaining exposure or control when either is inadequate.

decisionNodes.explanation: The decisive finding is the combination of the two injection origins and their separate hepatic versus duodenal connections, together with the visible open ends. Escape around an injected opening alone could be reflux and would not establish this pattern. Routine papillary diversion would address the distal system but not restore the absent connection to the hepatic ducts. Drain and arrange specialist transfer within the stated expertise limit. Further proximal dissection solely to complete a local injury description is unnecessary here; conversion remains appropriate when required for exposure or control. Repair timing and method belong to the HPB team.

record.title: Mapping recurrent bile at the duct-opening checkpoint
fairness: Reviewed the current salvage candidate's presentation, update, task, options and explanation, including the matching finite presentation. The four active nodes are the review population. The 103 kept audit occurrences, archived earlier versions and parked/held records are noted but not scored. Author self-checks, earlier review verdicts and the review-only key position are not evidence for this verdict.

One defensible best answer among the stated approaches: transcystic contrast cholangiography. Recurrent fluid away from the deliberate ductotomy and an unbroken gallbladder create concern for another bile source; the learner must choose an investigation of continuity/extravasation and then account for the clip-relative route. This is moderately demanding procedural application, not a hard item.

The gallbladder-side clip is a real anatomical discriminator, not merely an option-eliminating negative: injection into the gallbladder as currently configured would encounter that closed outlet. Removing the clip would be a different, unstated plan. The accessible duct opening supports the offered route without requiring blind additional dissection.

The fluorescence choice is credible because ICG has already been administered and the equipment is present. The explanation appropriately retains fluorescence as an adjunct rather than claiming that it is universally useless. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the exact comparative imaging recommendation was not independently source-verified in this offline review.

Cue attack: the labels have parallel acquisition grammar and comparable specificity. The two contrast options share their modality wording, so component convergence does not uniquely assemble the key. The clip and catheter findings make a route usable, but do not by themselves resolve contrast versus fluorescence. Listing both imaging systems avoids a key-only equipment permission. No unacceptable nonmedical wording shortcut found.

The live ambulatory cholecystectomy checkpoint is plausible with the explicitly supplied imaging resources. The green fluid, intact wall, clip and accessible opening are observable intraoperative findings. No image is promised but missing: the task selects an acquisition, not an interpretation of an unseen cholangiogram. Priya's age/sex and procedural frame are consistent.

Sequence check: choosing the study can naturally precede the next node's acquired injection findings. This explanation discusses the imaging purpose without revealing the later duct pattern, transfer decision or repair. It does not require the later result to solve this node. Bile-duct injury recognition and intraoperative mapping are high-yield general-surgery concepts.

PASS is an editorial judgment on the supplied text, not clinical approval, source verification or certification of live procedure sequencing. The candidate remains needs_clinician_review. No network, Git or runtime testing was used.
suggestions: Retain the clip position, accessible opening and both imaging alternatives; deleting those facts to reduce apparent cueing would remove legitimate procedural reasoning.
Optional concision: state the opening's position relative to the clip once, preserving that it is accessible without traction. The repeated position is not a blocking cue.
Preserve the transition as an actual acquisition followed by a new decision; do not display the second node's injection findings before this answer.

record.title: Unexplained bile during neck dissection
clarityIssues: The update says the surgeon cannot see the stream's origin, but the suture option refers to 'the leaking opening' and the explanation refers to 'An observed opening'. No opening has actually been observed in the supplied scene. This makes the distractor internally unavailable and makes the feedback misdescribe the evidence.

'Convert access' is an unnecessarily indirect way to say convert to open surgery. 'Explore the leaking hilar ducts' also presupposes localization beyond the visible finding medial to the gallbladder neck.

The task identifies the patient, operation and dissection stage adequately. The named 49-year-old woman, short complaint and explicit live ambulatory OR frame are appropriate; no pediatric issue applies. The decision-critical fluid observation is visible in text and does not require an invented image.

cues.phrase: The surgeon cannot see where the stream originates.
cues.why: Against 'Close the leaking opening with laparoscopic sutures', this permits nonmedical elimination: the surgeon cannot close a specific opening that has not been found. Retain genuine uncertainty, but replace the distractor or consistently describe an actually visible defect.

cues.phrase: Pause and obtain intraoperative contrast cholangiography
cues.why: This is the only pause-and-investigate option, facing completion, immediate closure and exploration. A reader can favor checking an unexplained problem before committing to treatment without interpreting biliary anatomy. 'Pause' uniquely advertises caution; the issue is the option set, not excessive key length.

fairness: Contrast cholangiography is a defensible best answer among these options for unexplained bile during dissection. I identify no confident clinical error in that core teaching point. The intact gallbladder observation is useful and should not be deleted merely to make the item harder.

The current alternatives do not create two consequential resident-level steps. Recognizing an unexplained bile source immediately selects the only diagnostic option; two treatments presume a localized lesion and completion ignores the new finding. High-yield injury recognition is being tested as a straightforward safety rule.

An elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is a plausible ASC procedure. Onsite contrast cholangiography requires appropriate imaging equipment and skill, neither established by the visible phrase 'ambulatory OR'. This is a capability uncertainty, not proof that the setting is wrong. The item must be restricted to a suitably equipped live setting or have that routine facility context available without a key-specific permission sentence.

As the first node, this should lead naturally to diagnostic mapping. Its explanation does not reveal the later transfer answer, which is good; however, the next node's exposed tissue-loss injury needs an explicit chronology bridge.

Scope: all three proposed executable nodes were reviewed, using their candidate presentation/profile, update, exhibit, task, option labels and explanation. The 103 Keep records and the recorded parked/held historical material were noted but not re-reviewed or counted. Review-only key markers and author self-assessments were not treated as evidence of quality.

This is an offline editorial review under question-authoring.2026-11-08.v15, including its owner lessons. No network or current-source verification was performed. decisionNodes.stem: Which initial strategy is most appropriate for {patientName}'s newly observed sigmoid wall defect during colonoscopy?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During sigmoid insertion, a 7-mm wall opening exposes yellow peritoneal fat. The adjacent edges are pink and mobile; the prepared lumen contains clear fluid. Blood pressure remains at baseline and the abdomen is soft. Insufflation is stopped, luminal fluid is suctioned and intravenous fluids and antibiotics are started while hospital transfer is coordinated.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic clip closure of the sigmoid defect
answerChoices.rationale: The newly seen small gap, mobile edges, clean lumen and preserved physiology support a prompt endoscopic closure attempt. Hospital monitoring and surgical consultation still follow.

answerChoices.label: Inpatient observation of the sigmoid defect
answerChoices.rationale: Monitored nonoperative care fits selected sealed injuries. This accessible gap remains open during the procedure, so leaving it unclosed gives up a feasible opportunity to limit leakage.

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic suture closure of the sigmoid defect
answerChoices.rationale: Operative closure is important when endoscopic treatment is unsuitable or fails. The small clean defect and mobile margins support an endoscopic attempt before committing to an operation.

decisionNodes.explanation: A visible opening into the peritoneal space is a wall breach. Its small size, clean field, mobile margins and prompt recognition support endoscopic clipping. decisionNodes.stem: Which immediate plan is most appropriate for {patientName}'s new abdominal and cardiopulmonary changes at the end of colonoscopy?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During placement of the final clips, the abdomen becomes progressively distended. At the immediate reassessment, the clip line holds the defect edges together, but the abdomen is taut and tympanitic, blood pressure falls and assisted ventilation is difficult. The airway is patent and breath sounds remain bilateral. Insufflation remains stopped; airway and circulatory support continue and the receiving hospital has been contacted.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous release of intraperitoneal gas followed by hospital transfer
answerChoices.rationale: The rapidly expanding tympanitic abdomen with simultaneous circulatory and ventilatory decline points to pressurized gas outside the bowel. Percutaneous decompression addresses that compartment before departure, while shared resuscitation and hospital escalation continue.

answerChoices.label: Orogastric tube decompression followed by supported hospital transfer
answerChoices.rationale: Gastric tube decompression targets gas within the stomach. It does not release pressurized intraperitoneal gas after a colonic breach, so it does not address the new combined findings before transfer.

answerChoices.label: Direct hospital transfer with ongoing airway and circulatory support
answerChoices.rationale: The patient still needs hospital source-control assessment. Direct departure with supportive treatment leaves the immediate pressure problem unrelieved; decompression should precede departure in this constructed clinical pattern.

decisionNodes.explanation: Gas that escaped before insufflation stopped can remain outside the bowel after clip apposition. Here, abdominal expansion is evolving during the final closure steps and produces a new combined ventilatory and circulatory problem at reassessment. Emergency percutaneous decompression precedes transfer while airway and circulatory support continue. Improvement is temporization and does not establish a durable seal or remove the need for hospital assessment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which immediate plan is most appropriate for {patientName}'s new abdominal and cardiopulmonary changes at the end of colonoscopy?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During placement of the final clips, the abdomen becomes progressively distended. At the immediate reassessment, the clip line holds the defect edges together, but the abdomen is taut and tympanitic, blood pressure falls and assisted ventilation is difficult. The airway is patent and breath sounds remain bilateral. Insufflation remains stopped; airway and circulatory support continue and the receiving hospital has been contacted.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous release of intraperitoneal gas followed by hospital transfer
answerChoices.rationale: The rapidly expanding tympanitic abdomen with simultaneous circulatory and ventilatory decline points to pressurized gas outside the bowel. Percutaneous decompression addresses that compartment before departure, while shared resuscitation and hospital escalation continue.

answerChoices.label: Orogastric tube decompression followed by supported hospital transfer
answerChoices.rationale: Gastric tube decompression targets gas within the stomach. It does not release pressurized intraperitoneal gas after a colonic breach, so it does not address the new combined findings before transfer.

answerChoices.label: Direct hospital transfer with ongoing airway and circulatory support
answerChoices.rationale: The patient still needs hospital source-control assessment. Direct departure with supportive treatment leaves the immediate pressure problem unrelieved; decompression should precede departure in this constructed clinical pattern.

record.title: New cardiopulmonary compromise during closure
fairness: Percutaneous release of intraperitoneal gas before supported transfer is the best offered plan for the combined taut tympanitic abdomen, falling blood pressure and difficult ventilation after a colonic breach. Orogastric decompression treats a different compartment; departure with resuscitation but no pressure relief leaves the immediate reversible problem untreated.

Two consequential steps remain: identify the pressure-producing compartment from the simultaneous abdominal and cardiopulmonary findings despite apparent clip apposition, then prioritize decompression before transport. The competing errors are treating all distension with a gastric tube and treating necessary hospital transfer as a substitute for immediate stabilization. This is moderate recognition-and-sequencing difficulty, not a hard differential-diagnosis item. Emergency response to endoscopic perforation and pressure compromise is high yield.

Cue attack: 'taut and tympanitic' is a clinical discriminator, not a nonmedical synonym for the uniquely keyed action. 'The airway is patent and breath sounds remain bilateral' supports localization without naming the diagnosis; it does not exclude every other cardiopulmonary cause. All three choices include hospital transfer and have comparable length. The key is not uniquely comprehensive because airway and circulatory support are explicitly shared. No rhetorical absolute, diagnosis label, teaching sentence or majority-component shortcut selects it.

The sequence is coherent: a recognized defect is clipped, abdominal distension evolves during the final steps, and new instability is assessed before departure. The update does not describe a long stable interval followed by unexplained new insufflation. The explanation locates escaped gas before insufflation stopped and does not equate successful edge apposition with elimination of extraluminal gas. This is clinically plausible; the visible text alone cannot establish the exact timing or volume of gas escape.

The preceding explanation does not teach percutaneous decompression. Removing the new update removes the indication for this rescue, so the follow-up earns a distinct decision. The adult patient identity is preserved. Emergency temporization in the ASC followed by hospital assessment fits the program; major surgical source control is not portrayed as a local procedure. decisionNodes.stem: At that hospital reassessment after sigmoid clip closure, which plan best fit {patientName}'s clinical and CT findings?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At the first hospital reassessment after clip closure of a small sigmoid defect, discomfort was improving. The abdomen was soft with localized tenderness; blood pressure and temperature were normal. CT with intravenous and water-soluble rectal contrast showed pericolic gas without extravasation or free fluid. Oral intake was withheld, and intravenous fluids and antibiotics had begun.

answerChoices.label: Inpatient observation with serial clinical examinations
answerChoices.rationale: Residual gas does not by itself establish closure failure. Taken together, the improving symptoms, soft abdomen and completed contrast study support inpatient monitoring with the treatment already started.

answerChoices.label: Repeat colonoscopy to reassess the clipped defect
answerChoices.rationale: Repeat instrumentation is not required solely for residual gas when the clinical and CT assessment supports observation. A specific residual closure problem may need specialist endoscopic reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic exploration with reinforcement of the closure
answerChoices.rationale: Surgical reassessment is important for deterioration, peritoneal signs or an ongoing leak. Residual gas in this improving patient does not establish those indications.

decisionNodes.explanation: Free gas can remain after an injury has been closed. The clinical trajectory, examination and contrast CT support inpatient monitoring with the treatment already started. They do not prove a durable seal. New peritoneal signs, worsening physiology or demonstrated leakage would require urgent surgical reassessment.

Equating extraluminal gas with automatic surgery is a recognizable high-yield error. Cue attack: 'discomfort was improving' and 'without extravasation or free fluid' are needed clinical discriminators rather than pre-answer teaching. They do not literally repeat the observation option. The three plans are comparable in specificity and length, with no diagnostic label revealing the key, rhetorical absolute, explanatory distractor or convergence pattern. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The endoscopist inspects the gastroesophageal junction after lavage.
decisionNodes.stem: During {patientName}'s EGD, which endoscopic plan should be used for the gastroesophageal lesion at this checkpoint?

exhibit.caption: Constructed endoscopy observations; written record, not an endoscopic image
cells: A narrow longitudinal mucosal split crosses the gastroesophageal junction. A small exposed vessel lies within the split; the surrounding mucosa has no ulcer crater.
The vessel and the rest of the split remain dry. No fresh blood accumulates in the stomach.

answerChoices.label: Observe the gastroesophageal lesion
answerChoices.rationale: The observations fit a dry Mallory-Weiss tear. CAG conditionally advises against routine hemostasis for its nonbleeding vessel; the ulcer visible-vessel rule should not be transferred automatically.

answerChoices.label: Clip the gastroesophageal lesion
answerChoices.rationale: Clipping treats active tear bleeding, but the current record is dry. A visible vessel in a peptic ulcer would justify intervention; this mucosal split is a different lesion.

answerChoices.label: Band the gastroesophageal lesion
answerChoices.rationale: Band ligation is an accepted method for active Mallory-Weiss bleeding. It does not become indicated merely because the vessel in this dry split is at the gastroesophageal junction.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is a dry junctional mucosal tear rather than an ulcer crater. Observation is supported at this checkpoint; a nonbleeding vessel does not automatically carry the peptic-ulcer treatment rule. CAG's recommendation is conditional and based on very low-certainty evidence, so this is not a universal prohibition on individualized hemostasis.

record.title: A dry junctional lesion
fairness: Reviewed the current v1 candidate presentation, update, exhibit, task, option labels and explanation. The two consequential operations are identifying the retching-associated junctional tear from its morphology and then deciding whether its dry exposed vessel warrants intervention. The peptic-ulcer visible-vessel treatment rule supplies a credible competing error. This is moderate application, not a hard technical endoscopy problem.

Observation is a defensible best routine local endoscopic plan in the stated stable, nonbleeding setting. Clipping and banding are credible interventions for a bleeding tear, but the current field does not show active hemorrhage. The explanation correctly limits its recommendation rather than claiming that individualized hemostasis is universally wrong. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. I have not independently verified the cited CAG recommendation or its exact exceptions in this offline review; its reported very low certainty remains a clinical-sign-off limitation.

The visible vessel keeps treatment plausible despite the dry field. The absence of an ulcer crater is necessary lesion discrimination, not an inappropriate negative to delete. The three options have parallel verb/site construction and comparable length. Observation versus intervention is the actual clinical decision; being the only observation option is not by itself a nonmedical answer cue. No reliable wording-only shortcut was found.

The live scene is plausible for scheduled ambulatory EGD after limited blood-streaked emesis with stable procedural observations and unchanged outpatient hemoglobin. It does not depict active hospital-level resuscitation in an ASC. The written exhibit clearly supplies the lesion architecture and reassessment after irrigation; it does not purport to be an actual endoscopic image. This supports record interpretation, not image-recognition assessment.

Elena Price is consistently a 48-year-old woman; the two-word complaint fits the visit. The task identifies the patient, procedure and local lesion decision and remains complete when separated from the presentation. Single-node case; no subsequent-step coherence issue or pediatric-parent requirement. No diagnostic test option or fixed testing duration appears in these visible fields.

Mallory-Weiss recognition and distinguishing its management from ulcer stigmata are high-yield general-surgery knowledge. The exact low-certainty nonbleeding-vessel recommendation is narrower than that broad topic; highYield does not assert measured ABSITE question frequency.

Report scope: reviewed all three proposed executable nodes, including the two marked previously passed, from the current candidate fields. The 55 kept records and 11 held/superseded planning records were noted and excluded from scored verdicts; historical snapshots and author quality assertions were not evidence of a pass. No network verification was performed. All three remain needs_clinician_review; editorial PASS is not Melissa Rowland's clinical approval.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between routine local observation and a categorical prohibition on hemostasis, including the explicit evidence-certainty caveat.

At clinical sign-off, confirm the exact recommendation and relevant recurrent-bleeding or coagulation exceptions. Do not turn this local endoscopic decision into an unsupported discharge decision or invent a timing or laboratory cutoff.

record.title: A dry junctional lesion
fairness: The resident must identify a retching-associated junctional mucosal tear from the longitudinal split, then decide whether a nonbleeding exposed vessel warrants local treatment in this lesion. Applying the familiar peptic-ulcer visible-vessel rule is a credible competing error. This is moderate application, not a hard device-selection problem.

Observation is the defensible preferred routine endoscopic plan for the stable, dry lesion described. The exposed vessel makes intervention tempting; the absence of an ulcer crater is decision-critical rather than an instruction that all nonbleeding vessels should be observed. Clipping and banding remain reasonable treatments in a different, actively bleeding tear scenario.

The explanation appropriately describes the recommendation as conditional and very low certainty and does not declare individualized hemostasis universally wrong. answerChoices.label: Endoscopic band ligation

answerChoices.label: Deploy a dedicated covered esophageal hemostasis stent

answerChoices.label: Repeat band ligation of the distal esophageal varices
answerChoices.rationale: Repeat ligation can treat a visible, capturable recurrent varix. Here suction exposes continued bleeding but blood again covers the column outlines and band margins. Repeating capture-based treatment is less appropriate than temporary tamponade in this recorded field.

answerChoices.label: Inject sclerosant into the distal esophageal varices
answerChoices.rationale: Sclerotherapy can use a visible variceal column as its treatment target; it does not universally require a single pinpoint vessel. The current record describes the columns themselves disappearing beneath blood after suction, so the earlier ligation-fallback role does not establish a safe injection site here.

decisionNodes.explanation: Persistent bleeding after attempted ligation and vasoactive therapy calls for temporary control while the hospital prepares definitive rescue. A dedicated removable covered esophageal hemostasis stent provides tamponade; it does not decompress the portal circulation. Balloon tamponade is another possible bridge. Reassessment for bleeding and device migration remains necessary. The distinction from sclerotherapy here is obscuration of the variceal columns themselves, rather than absence of a single pinpoint bleeding site.

decisionNodes.stem: At this checkpoint in {patientName}'s ERCP record, which intervention should the hospital team have selected?

exhibit.caption: Constructed hospital ERCP record: before scope withdrawal
cells: Contrast injected through the biliary catheter outlines the distal duct above the papilla, then escapes through the upper cut edge into a small retroperitoneal pocket.
A small separation is visible at the upper incised papillary margin. The remaining inspected duodenal wall is intact.
The guidewire remains within the bile duct and an intrahepatic branch.
Blood pressure and oxygenation remain stable without vasopressors or increased respiratory support.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic transpapillary plastic-stent placement
answerChoices.rationale: The observed cut-margin escape, stable physiology and retained intraductal wire support a plastic biliary stent for internal diversion with inpatient care.

answerChoices.label: Operative duodenal exploration and repair
answerChoices.rationale: Operation can be required for uncontrolled injury or deterioration. The current findings support an initial nonsurgical strategy, with the surgical team still involved.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drain placement
answerChoices.rationale: A transhepatic biliary route can help when internal drainage cannot be established. The retained intraductal wire already supplies access across the papilla, so a new transhepatic route is not the preferred offered starting plan.

answerChoices.label: ERCP stent exchange for biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Stent position does not establish current flow, and reassessing duct drainage may still be necessary. Exchanging a biliary stent does not evacuate the demonstrated extraluminal cavity, which is the source-control target asked about here.

record.title: Initial diversion for a recognized ERCP injury
fairness: The visible record supports one best offered intervention: endoscopic transpapillary plastic-stent placement. Contrast escape through the incised papillary margin and the corresponding visible separation establish a limited sphincterotomy-related injury; stable physiology and retained intraductal access support initial internal diversion. Operative repair and transhepatic drainage are real alternatives in different circumstances but are not equally preferred at this checkpoint. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the key or explanation.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret the cut-margin and contrast observations to distinguish this injury pattern from a larger duodenal-wall injury, then combine physiology and established biliary access to choose the initial intervention. Treating any extraluminal contrast as an automatic indication for surgery, or choosing a new drainage route despite usable internal access, are credible resident errors. Moderate difficulty is justified; the broad procedural alternatives do not make this a hard technical ERCP item.

The cue attack found no robust nonmedical shortcut. 'The guidewire remains within the bile duct and an intrahepatic branch' is necessary access information, not an explicit permission to select the key. 'The remaining inspected duodenal wall is intact' and stable anesthesia observations distinguish injury extent and urgency; they do not name the treatment. All three options name actual interventions with comparable length and specificity. None contains an explanatory warning, rhetorical absolute, uniquely comprehensive plan or component-convergence pattern.

Sphincterotomy followed by extraction is explicit and procedurally coherent. The injected structure, escape site, visible papillary finding and anesthesia course are available before scope withdrawal. The constructed record table makes the decision-critical findings accessible without claiming to supply an actual fluoroscopic image. Shared antibiotics, fasting, fluids, monitoring and surgical consultation prevent the key from winning merely by including routine supportive care.

Michael Nolan is a named 64-year-old man attending clinic to review an outside hospital record. The short complaint, demographic context and complete historical task are appropriate. This does not require an ambulatory center to provide ERCP rescue or inpatient management. Pediatric age and parent rules are inapplicable. The subsequent node explicitly records plastic-stent placement before reassessment, so its chronology agrees with this intervention; this explanation does not disclose the later collection-drainage answer.

Recognition and initial management of ERCP perforation are useful, high-yield surgical complication concepts. This PASS ranks the offered interventions; it does not establish plastic-stent superiority over every unoffered endoscopic technique. This is an offline editorial review of the candidate presentation, update, exhibit, task, choices and explanation. No external source verification or clinical approval was performed; the exact draft remains needs_clinician_review.

clarityIssues: 'Immediately after stone extraction and biliary sphincterotomy' leaves the procedural order unstated and lists extraction first. Specify sphincterotomy followed by extraction if that is the intended record; this wording does not establish that the procedure was actually performed in the wrong order.

'A small contrast pocket appears outside the distal bile duct beside the sphincterotomy' and 'The abnormality is at the sphincterotomy' do not clearly distinguish the observed leak origin from the author's localization conclusion. The reader should know what was injected and what the endoscopist actually saw at the cut margin.

'Blood pressure and ventilation remain near their preprocedure course' uses an undefined baseline to establish stability. State the observed stable anesthesia course directly; no invented numeric threshold is needed.
'Endoscopic transpapillary bile diversion' names a strategy rather than the actual intervention. The next node introduces a plastic stent although the selected action never specifies one.
fairness: Initial endoscopic biliary diversion is a defensible best answer if the intended finding is a limited sphincterotomy-related periampullary leak with stable physiology and maintained duct access. This is a precision concern, not a claim that the intended management is wrong.

The outside-hospital record setting is appropriate; this complication is not being treated in an unsupported ambulatory room. The procedure-to-inpatient-care progression is plausible, and adult demographics are consistent.

The clinically important concept is high-yield; precise advanced-endoscopic device comparisons should not be substituted for general surgical decision making.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The left TAPP peritoneal flap is open, exposing the deep ring and lateral preperitoneal tissue. Pink sigmoid forms part of the sac's posterior boundary: its wall and mesocolon move with the peritoneal reflection. With gentle medial traction, tissue along the lateral wall stretches taut while the neck remains broad and slack.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next maneuver should be used for Mateo's sigmoid-containing sac at this left TAPP repair checkpoint?

answerChoices.label: Mobilize the parietal attachments and reduce sac with sigmoid
Peel the sigmoid from the posterior peritoneal boundary and reduce it separately
Incise the deep ring margin and reduce the bowel-bearing sac together

decisionNodes.explanation: In this TAPP view, the sigmoid and mesocolon form a bowel-bearing sac boundary. The traction response locates the remaining restraint in the lateral attachments, with a slack neck. Mobilize those attachments from the preperitoneal side and bring the unit inward. Peeling the visceral boundary mistakes it for an adhesion; ring enlargement targets a different cause of resistance.
sourceLabels: Surgical Endoscopy / International Endohernia Society (2011); 10.1007/s00464-011-1799-6
Journal of Abdominal Wall Surgery / HerniaSurge Collaboration (2023); 10.3389/jaws.2023.11195

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The sigmoid and bowel-bearing proximal sac are now inside the abdomen. An empty peritoneal cuff just distal to the deep ring is clear of bowel, vas and vessels. The residual sac extends into the upper scrotum. Under magnification, traction-countertraction and blunt spreading expose a fibrotic patch in which vas and spermatic veins lie within the sac wall; its surfaces do not separate when traction is reversed.
decisionNodes.stem: How should Mateo's residual sac be handled at this left TAPP repair checkpoint after proximal reduction?

answerChoices.label: Divide at the free cuff and leave the adherent distal sac
Retract the cuff and sharply release the distal sac from cord
Add an inguinal incision and release the distal sac under direct vision

decisionNodes.explanation: The deciding finding is vas and veins incorporated in a fibrotic distal sac wall after a gentle plane-seeking attempt, with a separate empty cuff available proximally. Divide through that cuff and leave the adherent portion. Continued release through the shared wall risks cord injury, and additional access does not make complete release obligatory. Retained distal sac may form a seroma; evidence comparing strategies is limited.
sourceLabels: Surgical Endoscopy / International Endohernia Society (2011); 10.1007/s00464-011-1799-6
Journal of Abdominal Wall Surgery / HerniaSurge Collaboration (2023); 10.3389/jaws.2023.11195

record.title: Adherent distal sac: balancing completion against cord injury
fairness: Reviewed the current v1.r1 node with the current first-node presentation and explanation. The update explicitly establishes proximal reduction, an empty cuff and persistent distal adherence after a gentle plane-seeking attempt; it does not require remembering an unstated earlier result.

Division at the free cuff with retention of the adherent distal sac is the best offered action. The consequential interpretation is that further complete separation threatens cord structures despite attempted exposure; the subsequent decision is to accept a retained distal sac rather than pursue complete removal through that interface or add access solely to accomplish it.

The free-cuff observation is essential to the safety of the proposed division and should not be deleted as a cue. Both the key and sharp-release option reference the cuff. The three labels are comparable operative actions without explanatory qualifiers or a uniquely comprehensive key.

The alternatives are meaningfully inferior under the supplied shared fibrotic interface: sharp release is not merely an untried gentle maneuver, and an inguinal incision does not itself establish a safer separable plane. Changing the update to a readily separable distal plane would change this ranking; the upper-scrotal extension alone would not justify the key.

The sequence is coherent: reduce the bowel-bearing proximal component, reassess the residual sac, then decide how much distal dissection to undertake. Prior feedback offers general tissue-preservation scaffolding but does not disclose this specific completion decision. The task names the patient, procedure and post-reduction stage.

This is a plausible ASC checkpoint without an established injury requiring hospital rescue. Cord preservation and the consequences of distal-sac dissection are high-yield. The explanation appropriately acknowledges possible seroma and limited comparative evidence rather than claiming that every scrotal sac must be divided.
suggestions: Optional clinical wording check at sign-off: confirm that 'vas and spermatic veins lie within the sac wall' accurately expresses the intended fibrotic incorporation. If the intended observation is inseparable adherence to the outer sac surface, say that precisely; do not imply this is normal sac-wall anatomy. This is a terminology check, not a confident finding of clinical inaccuracy.

record.title: Managing the distal sac after visceral reduction
clarityIssues: Attempted separation draws the vas and spermatic veins upward with the sac describes transmitted traction, but does not clearly distinguish ordinary traction during an unfinished dissection from a persistently inseparable or hazardous distal plane. The explanation upgrades this to cord tethering and observed cord attachments.
The key does not explicitly place transection at the described free peritoneal cuff; that important location appears only in the explanation.

cues.phrase: reduce the entire distal sac / excise the entire distal sac
cues.why: Both distractors emphasize complete removal, whereas the key uniquely retains tissue after a traction warning. The repeated entire makes the pair look like two versions of over-treatment rather than independently attractive decisions.

cues.phrase: A peritoneal cuff near the ring is separate from bowel, vas and vessels
cues.why: Combined with the distal traction sentence, this strongly outlines the limited-division answer. The free cuff is legitimate decision-critical information, not a fact to delete; the current alternative set does too little to require weighing its implication.

fairness: Leaving an adherent distal sac after division at a verified free cuff is clinically defensible, and the explanation appropriately acknowledges a seroma tradeoff and limited evidence. No universal requirement for full excision is justified here.

The exact ranking against Continue laparoscopic dissection and reduce the entire distal sac is insufficiently secured. That option could mean careful continued separation with countertraction, not necessarily persisting with injurious traction. On the visible findings alone, I cannot confidently exclude that interpretation; this is a fairness concern rather than a claim that the intended key is clinically wrong.

The node has a genuine potential two-step decision: distinguish the safe proximal cuff from the difficult distal plane, then choose the extent of sac handling. Moderate is a qualitative prediction, contingent on making the plane limitation unambiguous; ambiguity itself is not difficulty.

Sequence is coherent: the sigmoid is reduced before distal-sac transection is considered. The update supplies the relevant prior outcome and can stand alone with the task. Earlier feedback protects a bowel-bearing wall but does not prescribe distal-sac retention. The new update changes the decision and is necessary.
The named adult, elective ASC repair and scrotal extension fit the operative scene. This is a high-yield cord-protection decision, with no pediatric or hospital-only procedure mismatch.
suggestions: Describe the actual distal-plane finding after an appropriate attempt at separation, sufficient to distinguish hazardous adherence from transmitted traction during routine dissection. Use a clinician-supported observation, not an invented threshold or the conclusion that dissection is unsafe.
Anchor the proposed transection to the free cuff, with comparable specificity across all choices.

Replace the conversion-plus-total-excision foil with a genuinely credible alternative at this checkpoint if the evidence supports one. Do not imply that changing access inherently requires complete distal excision.

Preserve the natural proximal-to-distal sequence and the limited-evidence/seroma qualification in feedback. Have the clinician verify the exact boundary that makes continued laparoscopic reduction less appropriate.

In this TAPP view, the sigmoid and mesocolon form a bowel-bearing sac boundary. The traction response locates the remaining restraint in the lateral attachments, with a slack neck. Mobilize those attachments from the preperitoneal side and bring the unit inward. Peeling the visceral boundary mistakes it for an adhesion; ring enlargement targets a different cause of resistance.
The deciding finding is vas and veins incorporated in a fibrotic distal sac wall after a gentle plane-seeking attempt, with a separate empty cuff available proximally. Divide through that cuff and leave the adherent portion. Continued release through the shared wall risks cord injury, and additional access does not make complete release obligatory. Retained distal sac may form a seroma; evidence comparing strategies is limited.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At the outside hospital's working-port placement checkpoint, the existing camera-port view shows a newly inserted working cannula passing through the posterior peritoneum into a deep hematoma. record.title: Expanding deep hematoma after working-port placement
fairness: The outside operative/anesthesia record and its working-port checkpoint are explicit. The named adult attends clinic after a hospital-level operation; the question does not place colectomy or major vascular rescue in the clinic's ambulatory OR.

The decisive scene is visible in prose: an existing camera view, an outer cannula still traversing the posterior peritoneum at the suspected injury, a removed obturator, an expanding hematoma with incomplete exposure and recurrent hypotension after an initial response. This is an unusual but plausible access complication, and the text distinguishes the retained cannula from a mere historical instrument track.

answerChoices.label: Reapply perihepatic packing and defer direct venous repair
answerChoices.rationale: The posterior source persists during inflow occlusion and responds to compression. Repacking provides temporary control pending physiological correction and planning of any necessary advanced repair.

answerChoices.label: Mobilize the right lobe and attempt direct venous repair
answerChoices.rationale: Repair may ultimately be necessary, but current packing-responsive bleeding and worsening physiology favor temporary control. Mobilization can release tamponade and expose a difficult venous injury.

answerChoices.label: Ligate the right hepatic artery and inspect the liver wound
answerChoices.rationale: The regional responses argue against treating all residual blood as right hepatic arterial inflow. A variant artery remains a differential consideration, but an artery has not been identified as this posterior source.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Left-lobe mobilization pauses at a short vascular connective-tissue bridge. The superior parathyroid has been freed from the thyroid surface except for this bridge. Within it, a common arterial stem divides into one limb entering the parathyroid and one entering the thyroid at its capsule. Neither limb has been divided.
decisionNodes.stem: Which vessel-control plan should be used at the remaining attachment of {patientName}'s left superior parathyroid during thyroidectomy?

answerChoices.label: Ligate the thyroid-bound limb at the capsule, retaining the parathyroid-bound limb.
answerChoices.rationale: Individual division of the thyroid-bound limb after the bifurcation separates thyroid inflow from gland inflow. The parathyroid-bound limb and its connection to the common stem are retained.

answerChoices.label: Ligate the common arterial stem beside the capsule, retaining each distal limb.
answerChoices.rationale: Common-stem control leaves both distal limbs physically present but removes their shared inflow. Retaining distal vessels is not equivalent to retaining their upstream connection.

answerChoices.label: Ligate the entire bridge beside the capsule, retaining the freed parathyroid gland.
answerChoices.rationale: A bulk ligature around the whole bridge includes the bifurcation and the gland-side inflow. Its proximity to the thyroid surface does not make it equivalent to individual thyroid-limb division.

decisionNodes.explanation: Isolate the thyroid-bound limb after the bifurcation and divide it at the thyroid capsule. Preserve the parathyroid-bound limb and its upstream connection. A common-stem ligature interrupts both destinations; a ligature around the whole bridge can do the same even close to the thyroid.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At the pre-closure check after thyroid removal, the team examines the upper gland in the field and the lower-gland tissue on the fresh specimen. The portion used for frozen section is separate from the remaining lower-gland tissue.
decisionNodes.stem: Which plan should be used for the two left parathyroid glands at the pre-closure checkpoint of {patientName}'s thyroidectomy?

answerChoices.label: Retain the upper gland in situ and autotransplant the remaining lower-gland tissue into neck muscle.
answerChoices.rationale: The upper gland retains its pedicle and shows inflow after decompression, supporting in-situ retention. The remaining lower tissue is detached and sterile, with benign parathyroid reported in the sampled portion, supporting muscle autotransplantation of the remaining tissue.

answerChoices.label: Autotransplant the upper gland into neck muscle and submit the remaining lower-gland tissue in full for permanent histology.
answerChoices.rationale: Transplanting the upper gland would disregard its current attached perfusion response. Submitting all remaining lower tissue for permanent histology would also forfeit the salvage opportunity after the supplied benign parathyroid report.

answerChoices.label: Retain the upper gland in situ and submit the remaining lower-gland tissue in full for permanent histology.
answerChoices.rationale: Retaining the upper gland follows its current findings. Complete submission of the remaining lower tissue, rather than partial sampling followed by grafting, would remove the tissue available for salvage.

answerChoices.label: Autotransplant the upper gland into neck muscle and autotransplant the remaining lower-gland tissue into neck muscle.
answerChoices.rationale: Autotransplantation addresses the detached lower tissue. Removing the upper gland responds to its earlier discoloration rather than its retained pedicle and subsequent inflow response.

decisionNodes.explanation: The attached upper gland shows fresh inflow after decompression, supporting retention in situ. The remaining lower-gland tissue is detached and sterile, with benign parathyroid reported in the sampled portion, supporting salvage by muscle autotransplantation. Transplanting the upper gland would disregard its current response. Submitting all remaining lower tissue for permanent histology would forfeit that salvage option. These observations do not guarantee long-term gland or graft function.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During scope withdrawal, Ava develops noisy inspiratory effort that becomes silent, with opposite chest and abdominal movement and loss of the carbon-dioxide trace. The endoscope is removed and stimulation stops. Repositioning, two-person facemask oxygenation with positive pressure, and IV propofol have not restored air movement. Inspiratory effort persists as oxygen saturation falls; the team continues oxygenation maneuvers.
decisionNodes.stem: Which rescue drug should the anesthesia team administer now for Ava Bennett during the EGD?

answerChoices.label: Administer intravenous succinylcholine
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent functional closure after initial measures calls for neuromuscular relaxation while airway rescue continues.

answerChoices.label: Administer intravenous epinephrine
answerChoices.rationale: Systemic epinephrine can be appropriate for severe lower-airway bronchoconstriction or systemic hypersensitivity. It does not directly relax the sustained glottic closure described here.

answerChoices.label: Administer inhaled albuterol
answerChoices.rationale: Albuterol targets lower-airway bronchoconstriction; the ongoing inspiratory effort without airflow after airway maneuvers instead supports sustained upper-airway closure.

decisionNodes.explanation: The persistent inspiratory effort without airflow after initial measures supports severe laryngospasm. IV succinylcholine provides neuromuscular relaxation for this emergency; the team must restore ventilation and secure the airway as needed.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Ava previously made inspiratory efforts with no air movement. Rescue neuromuscular blockade and tracheal intubation restored ventilation. Then pink frothy fluid appears with bilateral crackles. Suctioning clears the tube. At the current recheck, the catheter passes freely, the lumen remains clear, chest rise is bilateral and end-tidal carbon dioxide is near its earlier level. Diffuse crackles persist and oxygen saturation remains below its earlier level despite high inspired oxygen. Tracheal ventilation continues while hospital transfer is arranged.
decisionNodes.stem: Which respiratory intervention should the anesthesia team prioritize for Ava Bennett at this EGD-room reassessment?

answerChoices.label: Apply positive end-expiratory pressure
answerChoices.rationale: A currently clear, ventilated airway with persistent hypoxemia and diffuse crackles supports a lung oxygenation problem needing end-expiratory pressure support.

answerChoices.label: Suction the tracheal airway
answerChoices.rationale: Suction was appropriate when fluid occupied the tube. The current recheck follows effective clearance and shows a clear lumen with ongoing ventilation; repeated clearance is not the priority for the persistent lung oxygenation problem.

answerChoices.label: Administer albuterol by inhalation
answerChoices.rationale: Albuterol treats bronchoconstriction; persistent hypoxemia with diffuse crackles after effective clearance and relief of upper-airway obstruction favors pulmonary support at this checkpoint.

decisionNodes.explanation: After effective tube clearance, the continuing oxygenation problem with diffuse crackles following obstructed inspiratory effort supports postobstructive pulmonary edema. Prioritize positive end-expiratory pressure for lung support while ventilation and hospital transfer continue; reassess the airway if secretions obstruct it again.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Noah develops increased airway pressure, prolonged expiration and bilateral expiratory wheezing. The tracheal-tube marking is unchanged, a suction catheter passes freely without retrieving secretions, and chest movement is symmetric. Surgery pauses, oxygen and manual ventilation continue, and anesthesia is deepened. decisionNodes.stem: Which medication is the first priority to relieve Noah Reed's current airflow limitation during inguinal hernia repair?

answerChoices.label: Administer inhaled albuterol
answerChoices.rationale: Effective airflow through a checked airway permits initial inhaled beta-agonist rescue for the current bronchoconstriction.

answerChoices.label: Administer intravenous epinephrine
answerChoices.rationale: Epinephrine remains a rescue option for severe or refractory obstruction, ineffective inhaled delivery or systemic hypersensitivity, with or without circulatory collapse. This initial checkpoint still has effective ventilation and preserved oxygenation/perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Administer intravenous magnesium
answerChoices.rationale: Magnesium is an escalation adjunct when conventional bronchodilation is insufficient, rather than a substitute for the first beta-agonist treatment here.

answerChoices.label: Administer inhaled ipratropium
answerChoices.rationale: Ipratropium can accompany a beta agonist in more severe pediatric bronchoconstriction; it is not the replacement first bronchodilator for this checkpoint.

decisionNodes.explanation: Prioritize inhaled albuterol for the current bronchoconstriction after the mechanical airway check. Ipratropium is an adjunct rather than a replacement first bronchodilator. Systemic escalation depends on severity, response and effective delivery; it does not invariably require circulatory collapse.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Noah's expiratory wheeze and air entry improve after albuterol and manual ventilation. The team resumes time-triggered, pressure-controlled mandatory ventilation. The pressure target and independently set inspiratory time are unchanged from the earlier stable ventilator period. End-tidal carbon dioxide is rising while arterial pressure remains stable.
decisionNodes.stem: Which ventilator setting should the anesthesia team change first for Noah Reed at this checkpoint during inguinal hernia repair?

answerChoices.label: Reduce the set respiratory frequency
answerChoices.rationale: With fixed inspiratory time, a lower mandatory frequency provides more expiratory time while preserving the existing inspiratory delivery interval. This addresses incomplete exhalation without shortening a breath that is still delivering flow.

answerChoices.label: Shorten the set inspiratory time
answerChoices.rationale: Shortening inspiration would also leave more time for expiration, but in this pressure-controlled child flow is still entering at cycling and delivered volume is already reduced. It sacrifices further inspiratory delivery at this checkpoint.

answerChoices.label: Increase the inspiratory pressure target
answerChoices.rationale: Increasing the target can raise delivered volume, but it does not correct the demonstrated incomplete exhalation and may increase the volume that must leave the obstructed lungs.

decisionNodes.explanation: The current record shows incomplete exhalation plus ongoing inspiratory flow at time cycling with reduced delivered volume. Reduce mandatory frequency to provide expiratory time while preserving the inspiratory interval. Shortening inspiration can further reduce volume in this pressure-controlled setting; raising pressure does not resolve incomplete emptying. Reassess gas exchange and circulation.

case.presentation: {patientName}, an 11-year-old girl with established EoE, is undergoing EGD in the clinic's endoscopy room to reassess persistent solid-food dysphagia before selecting further treatment. At the earlier on-budesonide response endoscopy, an ultrathin gastroscope reached the stomach and proximal and distal biopsies showed rare eosinophils without active epithelial injury. Today the endoscopist is using a standard diagnostic gastroscope. Liquids and saliva pass. Her father, Daniel Chen, joined the preparation discussion and waits onsite. A pediatric endoscopist, endoscopy nurse and pediatric anesthetist are present.
