answerChoices.label: Close the rectal stump and form an end colostomy
answerChoices.rationale: Hartmann reconstruction remains appropriate for a high-risk host or unstable physiology. This record supplies the selected conditions under which restoration of continuity is supported.

answerChoices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis with a diverting loop ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The host, physiology and bowel observations support primary restoration with proximal diversion in this selected patient.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A prepared colonoscopy had treated an actively bleeding ascending-colon diverticulum with clips. Later, recurrent large bloody stools required further transfusion and fluid replacement. Repeat CTA showed active contrast accumulation beside the marked ascending-colon site. The colon had again filled with blood and clot, and his blood pressure fell during further bleeding.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next hemostatic plan best fits {patientName}'s recurrent hospital bleeding?

answerChoices.label: Repeat full preparation and endoscopic hemostasis
answerChoices.rationale: Repeat colonoscopy is reasonable in selected stable prepared recurrences. The continuing significant blood loss and newly localized active source support radiologic hemostasis here.

answerChoices.label: Proceed directly to right colectomy for hemorrhage control
answerChoices.rationale: The localization makes surgery possible if needed. A radiologic treatment route remains to be attempted before surgical rescue.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to selective angiography with possible embolization
answerChoices.rationale: CTA localizes recurrent active bleeding after endoscopic treatment, and the continuing course is poorly suited to another preparation-dependent examination.

decisionNodes.explanation: The recurrence is ongoing and hemodynamically significant after attempted endoscopic treatment. CTA supplies a current anatomic target. Selective angiography with possible embolization is the proposed next route.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Embolization initially controlled the ascending-colon bleed, but transfusion-requiring hematochezia recurred despite repeat endoscopic and radiologic attempts. The team selected surgical rescue. A tagged red-cell study showed activity in the left pelvis only on delayed images; early images showed no focal activity. During recurrent bleeding, CTA showed new contrast entering the ascending-colon lumen and increasing on the next phase. Selective angiography showed extravasation from the matching right-colon branch. Upper endoscopy and terminal ileal inspection found no source. Sigmoid diverticula were also present.
decisionNodes.stem: Which resection best fits {patientName}'s subsequent hemorrhage-control decision?

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Unconfirmed delayed pelvic tracer and sigmoid diverticula do not outweigh current matching right-colon extravasation. Delayed-only scintigraphic location needs confirmation before directing segmental resection.

answerChoices.label: Right colectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Current dynamic ascending-lumen contrast and matching selective extravasation support the localized right-colon source despite unconfirmed delayed tracer elsewhere.

answerChoices.label: Subtotal colectomy
answerChoices.rationale: An unconfirmed delayed tracer location does not erase the credible current right-sided source. Greater extent is not earned merely by incidental sigmoid diverticula.

decisionNodes.explanation: A delayed-only tagged-cell location needs confirmation before directing segmental colectomy. Current dynamic CTA and matching selective angiography localize the ascending source more credibly here. Once surgery is selected after failed hemostatic attempts, right colectomy follows the credible localization. Genuinely unresolved current localization would require a different extent discussion.

decisionNodes.stem: Which vascular assessment should the hospital team perform at {patientName}'s recorded presentation?

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the injured leg
answerChoices.rationale: A warm foot and a palpable pulse do not complete this assessment. The asymmetric pulse and ABI below 0.9 support arterial imaging with CTA.

answerChoices.label: Repeat bedside ABI after observation
answerChoices.rationale: Repeat indices can follow an initially reassuring assessment. The current abnormal examination and index already warrant imaging.

answerChoices.label: Immediate arterial exploration before imaging
answerChoices.rationale: Exploration is appropriate for hard signs or a threatened limb. This stable patient lacks those findings and has a fracture that benefits from anatomic definition.

decisionNodes.stem: Which operative sequence best fits {patientName}'s new limb findings?

answerChoices.label: Temporary arterial shunt, fixation, then definitive repair
answerChoices.rationale: A temporary shunt restores flow while the unstable skeleton is addressed, allowing definitive reconstruction after stabilization. Viable but poorly perfused tissue makes reperfusion time consequential.

answerChoices.label: External fixation, then definitive arterial repair
answerChoices.rationale: Fixation before final repair can protect a reconstruction. It leaves an already ischemic limb without flow during that work.

answerChoices.label: Definitive arterial repair, then external fixation
answerChoices.rationale: Restoring definitive flow first can be reasonable when skeletal movement will not threaten the repair. Gross instability and required fixation favor temporary flow restoration before reconstruction.

decisionNodes.stem: Which vascular plan best fits {patientName}'s examination and recorded Doppler worksheet?

answerChoices.label: CT angiography before disposition
answerChoices.rationale: ABI is ankle systolic pressure divided by brachial systolic pressure: 120/150 = 0.80. The worksheet has inverted the ratio. This abnormal index warrants arterial imaging after penetrating extremity trauma despite the reassuring examination.

answerChoices.label: Observation with repeat Doppler pressures
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated measurements already agree; their interpretation, rather than an unconfirmed reading, is the unresolved problem. Observation and another ratio should not replace indicated evaluation of the documented abnormal index.

answerChoices.label: Discharge after the vascular assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Discharge criteria depend on a normal examination and a genuinely normal ABI. The raw pressures instead give 0.80, so the printed normal-looking ratio cannot justify this plan. Routine precautions are common to all plans and do not repair the abnormal assessment.

What are confidence intervals?

decisionNodes.stem: What conclusion about equivalence follows from this 90% confidence interval?

answerChoices.label: Evidence is inconclusive
answerChoices.rationale: The interval includes differences within the equivalence bounds and beyond the upper bound; it establishes neither equivalence nor non-equivalence.

answerChoices.label: Evidence supports equivalence
answerChoices.rationale: The upper endpoint +3 exceeds the prespecified +2-day bound, so the complete interval is not contained within the equivalence range.

answerChoices.label: Evidence supports non-equivalence
answerChoices.rationale: An endpoint beyond a margin does not exclude the equivalent differences also contained in this interval.

decisionNodes.explanation:
TOST equivalence requires the 90% CI to lie wholly within both prespecified bounds.
The interval -1 to +3 spans the +2-day bound: the equivalence result is inconclusive.
Crossing a bound does not establish non-equivalence when equivalent differences remain in the interval.

decisionNodes.stem: What happens to the confidence-interval width?

answerChoices.label: It becomes half as wide
answerChoices.rationale: With fixed SD and confidence level, width scales as 1/sqrt(n).

answerChoices.label: It becomes one-quarter as wide
answerChoices.rationale: This applies 1/n scaling rather than 1/sqrt(n).

answerChoices.label: It remains the same width
answerChoices.rationale: The confidence level is fixed but increased sampling reduces standard error.

decisionNodes.explanation:
With known SD and fixed confidence level, CI width is proportional to 1/sqrt(n).
New/old width = sqrt(100 / 400) = 1/2.
One-quarter confuses variance scaling with interval-width scaling.

decisionNodes.stem: What sample-size change does the normal-model formula require?

answerChoices.label: Four times as many observations
answerChoices.rationale: Required n is proportional to 1/(target difference squared).

answerChoices.label: Twice as many observations
answerChoices.rationale: This uses an inverse rather than inverse-square relationship.

answerChoices.label: Half as many observations
answerChoices.rationale: Smaller effects require more precision, not less information.

decisionNodes.explanation:
For this normal model, required n is proportional to 1/(target difference squared).
Halving the target difference multiplies n by 1/(1/2)^2 = 4.
Twice as many applies a linear relationship instead.

Twice as many applies a linear relationship instead.

decisionNodes.stem: Which available factor product best fits {patientName}'s urgent warfarin-reversal record?

answerChoices.label: Thawed plasma
answerChoices.rationale: Major warfarin-associated bleeding requires rapid replacement of deficient factors while source control and vitamin K proceed. Kcentra is generally useful for this purpose, but its label contraindicates it in known heparin-induced thrombocytopenia because it contains heparin. Among these stated products, plasma provides the needed broad factor replacement without that product-specific contraindication.

answerChoices.label: Four-factor PCC (Kcentra)
answerChoices.rationale: Four-factor PCC is a close and normally favored reversal choice. This specific product contains heparin and is contraindicated with the established HIT history in this record.

answerChoices.label: Recombinant activated factor VII
answerChoices.rationale: An activated single-factor product is not a comprehensive replacement for the warfarin-reduced vitamin K-dependent factors. Its use in selected inhibitor-associated bleeding is a different indication.

decisionNodes.stem: Which electrolyte prescription best fits {patientName}'s transfusion findings using his current vascular access?

answerChoices.label: Calcium gluconate through a monitored peripheral IV
answerChoices.rationale: Large citrate exposure can lower ionized calcium, impairing coagulation and cardiovascular function. The measured deficit requires IV calcium; with peripheral access, calcium gluconate is the better fit among these prescriptions. Calcium chloride is more irritating and is generally reserved for central administration. Continue ECG, access-site and ionized-calcium monitoring; these formulations are not dose-for-dose interchangeable.

answerChoices.label: Calcium chloride through a monitored peripheral IV
answerChoices.rationale: This supplies calcium, but the proposed peripheral route creates an avoidable tissue-injury concern compared with calcium gluconate. The objection is the actual prescription and access, not failure of chloride to correct hypocalcemia.

answerChoices.label: Magnesium sulfate through a monitored peripheral IV
answerChoices.rationale: Magnesium can be used for a demonstrated magnesium deficit and some arrhythmias, but it does not replace the directly measured severe ionized-calcium deficit in this transfusion record. A longer QT does not establish magnesium deficiency.

decisionNodes.stem: Which component action best fits {patientName}'s later traumatic-bleeding record under the cited European trauma guidance?

answerChoices.label: Give a platelet component now
answerChoices.rationale: The fibrinogen response does not resolve the platelet decision. A count of 78 x 10^9/L exceeds the usual ongoing-bleeding trauma target of 50, but the cited European guidance suggests a target above 100 with traumatic brain injury. The enlarging intracranial injury therefore changes the ranking toward platelets. This is a weak, low-certainty recommendation, not proof of outcome benefit from a universal TBI threshold; specialist reassessment remains essential.

answerChoices.label: Repeat the count before adding a platelet component
answerChoices.rationale: Serial reassessment is necessary, and 78 is above the guideline target for general ongoing traumatic bleeding. Waiting on that general target overlooks the simultaneously enlarging intracranial injury and the cited higher TBI target.

answerChoices.label: Give another cryoprecipitate component now
answerChoices.rationale: The fibrinogen concentration has responded. Further cryoprecipitate does not address the platelet target relevant to the enlarging traumatic intracranial injury.

decisionNodes.stem: Which RBC prescription best fits {patientName}'s later hospital assessment?

answerChoices.label: Give one RBC unit slowly; reassess before prescribing more
answerChoices.rationale: The current severe symptomatic anemia supports RBC transfusion despite the earlier reaction. The previous pressure/volume response and LV dysfunction argue for limiting volume exposure, using a slower controlled administration and reassessing after one unit. This avoids both withholding needed support and precommitting to a larger course. No exact rate or routine prophylactic-diuretic efficacy is assumed.

answerChoices.label: Give no RBCs now; reassess symptoms and hemoglobin
answerChoices.rationale: Avoiding exposure is tempting after a respiratory reaction, but it leaves severe symptomatic anemia untreated in the stated later stable assessment. The prior event should inform administration rather than automatically prohibit necessary RBC support.

answerChoices.label: Give two RBC units slowly; reassess after the course
answerChoices.rationale: Slowing administration addresses one risk, but a planned two-unit course adds volume before learning the response to the first unit in a patient with a prior congestion event. Single-unit reassessment is the better fit here.

decisionNodes.stem: Which donor-selection and compatibility plan best fits {patientName}'s later hospital RBC requirement?

answerChoices.label: Jka-negative RBCs with an antiglobulin serologic crossmatch
answerChoices.rationale: The negative current screen does not erase the clinically significant antibody history. Select donor cells lacking Jka and use serologic antiglobulin compatibility testing. decisionNodes.stem: Which anticoagulant action best fits {patientName}'s hospital platelet record while antibody testing is pending?

answerChoices.label: Stop heparin and start argatroban
answerChoices.rationale: The initial postoperative fall recovered before a new fall exceeding half the recovery count during the characteristic delayed heparin-exposure period. That trajectory warrants suspected-HIT management despite no detected thrombosis. Stop heparin and use an appropriate nonheparin anticoagulant while testing proceeds; argatroban is one supported option with the stated organ-function context. These observations do not exclude every alternative cause, and this item does not prescribe a universal intensity or claim agent superiority.

answerChoices.label: Replace unfractionated heparin with enoxaparin
answerChoices.rationale: Changing to low-molecular-weight heparin does not remove heparin exposure in suspected HIT. A different heparin formulation is not the protective substitution needed for this delayed pattern.

answerChoices.label: Withhold anticoagulants until antibody results return
answerChoices.rationale: The low platelet count does not eliminate the thrombotic risk of a credible HIT syndrome. In the supplied record there is no active bleeding to support simply leaving suspected HIT without an alternative anticoagulant while testing is pending.

decisionNodes.stem: Which anticoagulant plan best fits {patientName}'s hospital record after both assay results are available?

answerChoices.label: Stop argatroban and resume UFH prophylaxis
answerChoices.rationale: The delayed platelet course justified initial suspected-HIT treatment, but weak binding positivity does not establish pathogenic HIT antibodies. A valid negative functional result changes that assessment: most such patients do not have HIT and can be managed accordingly, including heparin if it remains indicated. Functional tests can be falsely negative, especially with a high-probability course and strongly positive immunoassay. The weak binding result here does not supply that strong-immunoassay conflict; clinical reassessment remains necessary.

answerChoices.label: Continue argatroban for presumed HIT
answerChoices.rationale: Interim argatroban was reasonable before confirmation. Continuing it as presumed HIT solely because of weak binding positivity disregards the valid negative functional assay. A strong immunoassay result with high clinical probability or concern about functional-assay validity would create a different conflict requiring specialist reconciliation.

answerChoices.label: Replace argatroban with warfarin for presumed HIT
answerChoices.rationale: This both carries forward an insufficiently supported HIT diagnosis and starts a VKA before platelet recovery. The question is the revised diagnostic basis for the anticoagulant, not convenience of an oral agent.

decisionNodes.stem: Which hemostatic plan best fits {patientName}'s planned oral procedure in the reviewed record?

answerChoices.label: VWF-containing concentrate with tranexamic acid
answerChoices.rationale: The initial VWF rise does not persist on the actual four-hour sample, so it does not establish a sustained useful desmopressin response for this procedure. The low baseline activity and prior significant dental bleeding also do not fit the mild, higher-baseline group for tranexamic acid monotherapy. VWF replacement with an antifibrinolytic adjunct is the best of these plans; the hematology plan must define product, targets and monitoring.

answerChoices.label: IV desmopressin with tranexamic acid
answerChoices.rationale: The early trial rise makes this a credible option, but the four-hour VWF result has returned near baseline despite a preserved factor VIII activity. Initial response is not the same as sustained VWF coverage.

answerChoices.label: Tranexamic acid monotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: This can be appropriate for selected minor mucosal procedures in patients with a mild phenotype and higher baseline VWF activity. The baseline 0.18 and prior persistent dental bleeding do not fit that narrower group. Local hemostasis remains common care but does not remove the systemic coverage decision.

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should precede another platelet-directed corticosteroid course for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Marrow aspirate/core biopsy with cytogenetics
answerChoices.rationale: A prior temporary platelet response does not establish that new multilineage cytopenias share the original peripheral mechanism. Low production and abnormal neutrophil morphology warrant integrated marrow assessment, including architecture and cytogenetics, before repeating platelet-directed treatment. Nutritional, medication and other mimics still require assessment; normal B12/folate do not exclude all reversible causes and no marrow diagnosis is proved by this record.

answerChoices.label: Peripheral-blood myeloid gene-panel sequencing
answerChoices.rationale: A clonal molecular finding can be useful, but a blood sequencing panel cannot substitute for the marrow morphology, architecture and integrated evaluation needed for this changed production pattern.

answerChoices.label: Peripheral-blood lymphoid flow cytometry
answerChoices.rationale: This is useful for a circulating lymphoid population, but the new low-production multilineage pattern with abnormal neutrophil morphology calls for marrow assessment rather than a blood lymphoid panel as its replacement.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next overall management recommendation should be made after reviewing {patientName}'s dialysis course?

answerChoices.label: Refer for parathyroidectomy assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Progressive severe symptomatic hyperparathyroidism despite documented treatment and dose-limiting toxicity supports surgical assessment alongside nephrology care. The constructed serial PTH values are not a universal operative cutoff.

decisionNodes.stem: Which offered bone-directed medicine is most appropriate to add for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Denosumab
answerChoices.rationale: Osteoporosis remains a separate target despite calcium control. Denosumab is an available PHPT bone-density treatment, avoiding the oral alendronate contraindication and the teriparatide warning for underlying PHPT. Calcium monitoring and individual planning remain necessary.

answerChoices.label: Oral alendronate
answerChoices.rationale: Alendronate is a credible PHPT skeletal treatment, but oral use is contraindicated with achalasia and delayed esophageal emptying.

answerChoices.label: Teriparatide
answerChoices.rationale: Teriparatide is a real osteoporosis medicine, but labeling advises avoiding an underlying hypercalcemic disorder such as PHPT. Cinacalcet-controlled calcium does not establish cure.

decisionNodes.stem: Which operative plan matches {patientName}'s recorded Miami protocol after the supplied samples?

answerChoices.label: Conclude parathyroid exploration
answerChoices.rationale: The highest baseline is 180; half is 90. The 10-minute value of 80 meets the Miami decline criterion despite remaining above the reference interval. This supports concluding exploration under that protocol, not a guarantee of cure.

answerChoices.label: Extend to bilateral neck exploration
answerChoices.rationale: Extension is credible after an inadequate decline, but these values meet the named protocol. Using 100 as the sole baseline or requiring laboratory normalization misclassifies the result.

answerChoices.label: Continue PTH sampling until laboratory normalization
answerChoices.rationale: Waiting for normalization applies a stricter endpoint than conventional Miami. Further sampling is real, but not required merely because 80 remains above the reference interval.

decisionNodes.stem: Which confirmation and source-assessment plan should {patientName} receive next?

answerChoices.rationale: This repairs exposure but substitutes a specialized ACTH-dependent investigation for the initial basal ACTH classification.

decisionNodes.stem: Which adrenal replacement plan should the founder recommend for {patientName}'s pending hospital discharge?

answerChoices.label: Hydrocortisone with endocrine reassessment of recovery
answerChoices.rationale: Prior autonomous cortisol excess suppressed ACTH drive and remaining cortisol reserve, so preserved anatomy does not justify omitting glucocorticoid replacement.

answerChoices.rationale: This is ACTH-related cortisol suppression; aldosterone is generally preserved, and mineralocorticoid replacement does not address the expected cortisol deficit.

decisionNodes.stem: Which aldosterone-directed treatment should {patientName} receive on this record?

answerChoices.label: Start spironolactone with potassium and creatinine monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Both samples are selective, but the aldosterone/cortisol ratio is 6 on each side. Without lateralization, targeted medical therapy is preferred to nodule-driven unilateral surgery.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with left adrenalectomy for the CT nodule
answerChoices.rationale: The left raw aldosterone is higher, but so is cortisol; corrected secretion is equal. The nodule does not establish a left functional source.

answerChoices.label: Repeat adrenal venous sampling before selecting treatment
answerChoices.rationale: The cortisol gradients establish bilateral sampling adequacy; nonlateralization is not itself technical failure.

decisionNodes.explanation: With cosyntropin, the right and left cortisol selectivity ratios are 10 and 20. The corrected aldosterone ratios are 1200/200 = 6 and 2400/400 = 6, so the larger left raw value does not show lateralization. Use a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with potassium and renal monitoring rather than operate on the CT nodule or repeat an adequate study.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial oncologic treatment sequence should be planned for {patientName} at the adrenal center?

answerChoices.label: Plan oncologic adrenal resection without preoperative needle biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: A localized primary adrenal malignancy pattern without prohibitive anatomical involvement supports an upfront complete-resection strategy; routine needle confirmation is not required.

answerChoices.label: Obtain adrenal core biopsy, then plan oncologic adrenal resection
answerChoices.rationale: Routine biopsy does not improve the required sequence for an apparently resectable suspected primary cortical malignancy.

answerChoices.label: Obtain adrenal core biopsy, then give etoposide/doxorubicin/cisplatin plus mitotane before reassessing resection
answerChoices.rationale: This is a systemic ACC pathway, but no distant disease or anatomy preventing initial complete resection is shown to justify making it mandatory before surgery here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The primary-adrenal malignant pattern must be interpreted with staging and anatomy. This record shows no distant disease, no great-vessel encasement or thrombus, and no multi-organ extension preventing an upfront surgical strategy. Plan expert oncologic resection without routine needle confirmation. Neoadjuvant treatment is considered when complete R0 resection is not initially feasible; size alone does not establish that condition. decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment sequence should be recommended for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Chemotherapy with trastuzumab/pertuzumab, then surgery
answerChoices.rationale: The substantial node-positive HER2-positive tumor supports a complete combined neoadjuvant regimen before the definitive operation.

answerChoices.rationale: It postpones the established combined systemic strategy until after resection in this node-positive substantial primary.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Ultrasound showed an impacted gallbladder-neck stone, wall thickening and surrounding fluid. Fever and focal tenderness continued after antibiotics. During observation, recurrent chest pressure coincided with new ST depression and a continuing troponin rise; echocardiography showed a new regional wall-motion abnormality. Blood pressure was falling despite fluids.
decisionNodes.stem: Alongside cardiac treatment and resuscitation, which immediate gallbladder plan best fit {patientName} at that checkpoint?

answerChoices.label: Immediate percutaneous gallbladder drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent gallbladder infection still needs source control while the new cardiac findings and circulatory deterioration make immediate general anesthesia hazardous. Drainage addresses that competing need.

answerChoices.label: Immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Definitive surgery is preferred for many patients with stable comorbidity, but the current dynamic ischemic findings and falling pressure are different from chronic risk.

answerChoices.label: Continued antibiotics with reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Concurrent cardiac treatment is necessary, but continuing fever and focal findings despite antibiotics leave gallbladder source control unresolved.

decisionNodes.explanation: There are two simultaneous problems: persisting gallbladder infection and new active myocardial ischemic findings with circulatory deterioration. The latter changes the immediate operative choice; it does not remove the need to address the infected compartment. Gallbladder drainage provides source control while cardiac care and resuscitation continue. This does not prescribe a post-infarction waiting interval or a cardiac drug regimen.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The ERCP followed fever, jaundice and rising cholestatic tests. Balloon and basket attempts did not remove the impacted stone. Contrast remained above it, and the guidewire lay beyond it in the proximal duct. During the attempts, blood pressure began falling and supplemental oxygen requirements increased.
decisionNodes.stem: Which drainage route best fits {patientName}'s current procedural findings while resuscitation continues?

answerChoices.label: Transpapillary plastic biliary stent
answerChoices.rationale: Failed extraction does not equal failed drainage access: the wire already crosses the obstruction. A temporary stent can use that access while definitive stone treatment is deferred.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drain
answerChoices.rationale: This is a real rescue route when endoscopic drainage cannot be established. The demonstrated transpapillary wire access supports using the less disruptive already-established route first.

answerChoices.label: Operative common-duct drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Operative drainage can be needed after less invasive routes fail or for another operative indication. Extraction failure with an accessed duct and deteriorating physiology does not establish that boundary.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the two different procedural outcomes: the stone was not extracted, but access across it was achieved. With deteriorating physiology, endoscopic stent drainage can use that access as a bridge. Failed extraction does not require abandoning endoscopic drainage for a new percutaneous or operative route. Definitive clearance and planned stent removal or exchange remain necessary after stabilization.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At readmission he had rigors, jaundice and rising cholestatic tests. CT showed the plastic stent in its prior position but increased upstream duct dilation. Fever and hypotension persisted after antibiotics and fluids. Repeat ERCP reached the papilla and passed a wire upstream alongside the stent; the old record still showed an uncleared stone.
decisionNodes.stem: Which immediate drainage plan best fits {patientName}'s readmission at this procedural checkpoint?

answerChoices.label: ERCP with biliary stent exchange
answerChoices.rationale: Stent position does not establish patency. New infection with upstream dilation requires renewed drainage, and the existing endoscopic access supports stent reassessment/exchange before switching route.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Percutaneous drainage is a useful rescue when endoscopic access or drainage fails. This wire already lies upstream, so an old stent failure does not itself require abandoning the endoscopic route.

answerChoices.label: Operative common-duct exploration and drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Operative exploration is a legitimate stone-clearance route, but current infected obstruction with renewed endoscopic access favors drainage rather than an immediate escalation to surgery.

decisionNodes.explanation: A correctly positioned bridge may still fail to drain. Interpret the new upstream dilation together with infection and deterioration, then distinguish prior device failure from failure of current endoscopic access. Renewed endoscopic drainage with stent reassessment/exchange is the best offered immediate plan. Definitive stone treatment and planned stent removal or exchange remain separate follow-up obligations; the exact maneuver depends on procedural findings.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The referring hospital reports a newly fixed tender right groin lump. {patientName} still passes stool and has not vomited. Contrast CT shows part of the bowel circumference entering a small opening below the inguinal ligament, medial to the common femoral vein. The remaining lumen stays in the abdomen. This does not claim that CT alone proves irreversible necrosis or choose a repair material.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: {patientName}'s outside operative record describes a perforated bowel segment within a femoral sac. Enteric contents spilled into the field before resection. Source control and lavage are complete, circulation is stable, and the groin defect measures 2 cm. The surgeon can approximate its edges without tension.
decisionNodes.stem: Which groin repair should be recommended for {patientName}'s recorded operative field?

answerChoices.label: Biologic mesh reinforcement of the defect
Primary tissue closure of the groin defect

decisionNodes.explanation: Gross spillage separates this case from controlled clean-contaminated bowel resection. WSES supports primary tissue repair when such a defect is small and directly closable. Its less-than-3-cm boundary directly supports this constructed 2-cm observation; the recommendation is older and low certainty, not a rule for all contaminated abdominal-wall defects.

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: The teaching record selected Permanent macroporous synthetic mesh repair.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: {patientName} has a primary reducing inguinal hernia that limits walking. He remains active without a cardiopulmonary limitation and follows instructions throughout the supine examination. An earlier prostate-cancer operative note describes dissection behind the pubic bone to the prostatic apex and creation of a vesicourethral anastomosis. The consulting surgeons regularly perform the offered repair and anesthesia combinations.
decisionNodes.stem: Which repair and anesthetic plan should be favored for {patientName}'s symptomatic primary inguinal hernia?

answerChoices.label: Lichtenstein mesh repair with general anesthesia
Totally extraperitoneal mesh repair with general anesthesia
Lichtenstein mesh repair with local infiltration

decisionNodes.explanation: The old operation used the retropubic/pelvic region, so primary-repair advice must be individualized rather than automatically applying the usual laparo-endoscopic preference. An offered anterior Lichtenstein repair is reasonable, and experienced local infiltration is favored for this cooperative reducing open-repair patient. Prior prostate surgery is not an absolute ban on expert laparoscopy, and neither general nor spinal anesthesia is universally contraindicated.

decisionNodes.stem: Which liberation plan best fits {patientName} at this recorded assessment?

answerChoices.label: Proceed to a monitored spontaneous breathing trial
answerChoices.rationale: Multidomain readiness and the observed comfortable sample support testing sustained breathing under minimal assistance.

answerChoices.label: Continue assist-control ventilation and reassess breathing tolerance
answerChoices.rationale: Deferral would be appropriate for actual instability or observed intolerance, neither of which is supplied by this completed measurement.

answerChoices.label: Use stepwise pressure-support reductions before a breathing trial
answerChoices.rationale: A gradual support-reduction pathway does not resolve a demonstrated barrier here and can defer the direct trial supported by the record.

decisionNodes.explanation: The readiness domains and observed tolerance support proceeding to a monitored SBT. AARC does not require RSBI as a gate to a trial; it also does not say to ignore actual intolerance. No new index cutoff or trial duration is prescribed.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next infusion adjustment best addresses {patientName}'s current hypoperfusion?

answerChoices.label: Add a dobutamine infusion
answerChoices.rationale: The new low flow and weak contraction accompany persistent hypoperfusion despite restored pressure and an assessment that does not support more fluid. Adding dobutamine to norepinephrine is a supported option for this phenotype.

answerChoices.label: Increase the norepinephrine infusion
answerChoices.rationale: The MAP target is achieved. Additional pressure support does not directly correct the newly demonstrated low flow and weak contraction.

answerChoices.label: Give a balanced-crystalloid bolus
answerChoices.rationale: The current reversible test shows no flow response, and the new cardiac findings identify a different support problem. Another empiric bolus is poorly supported by these observations.

decisionNodes.explanation: The pressure response has separated from the flow response. New low output and diffuse weak contraction accompany persistent hypoperfusion, while passive leg raising produces no flow increase. Adding dobutamine is a supported option in this setting, with reassessment of perfusion and adverse effects.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At clinic follow-up, {patientName}'s hospital record documents an intact appendectomy. The outside review examined one tip block containing low-grade mucinous lining. Expert permanent review of the entire specimen maps a separate proximal focus of irregular malignant glands infiltrating mesoappendiceal fat. The base margin is clear. Chest, abdominal and pelvic staging shows no distant lesions or deposits on serosal surfaces. Colonoscopy shows no separate colonic lesion. She has recovered and is fit for surgery.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s appendiceal tumor after the complete specimen review?

answerChoices.label: Surveillance after the appendectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The tip block does not represent the whole lesion. The separately mapped infiltrative focus changes the tumor classification and creates a regional nodal indication despite local margin clearance.

answerChoices.label: Right hemicolectomy with regional nodes
answerChoices.rationale: The complete specimen establishes invasive glandular disease beyond the nonrepresentative tip block. With no represented distant or serosal disease, regional resection and nodal assessment are appropriate even though the appendectomy margin is clear.

answerChoices.label: Cytoreduction with intraperitoneal chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Mesoappendiceal invasion is not the same finding as tumor deposits distributed on peritoneal surfaces. The current complete-specimen and staging record supports the regional pathway; cytoreduction and intraperitoneal treatment require a different disease distribution and specialist assessment.

decisionNodes.explanation: A benign-appearing or low-grade sampled region cannot classify unsampled parts of a heterogeneous appendix. The full specimen demonstrates infiltrative glandular disease. A clear base addresses the local margin; it does not address regional nodes. Mesoappendiceal invasion without demonstrated serosal dissemination supports right hemicolectomy rather than the peritoneal-disease pathway.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s abdominal-wall findings and functional complaint?

answerChoices.label: Start core rehabilitation; observe the focal navel defect at follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The broad intact midline and symptom response localize the functional problem away from the painless focal opening. Rehabilitation can be considered first while the reducible asymptomatic focal defect is observed.

answerChoices.label: Repair the focal navel defect; then start core rehabilitation at follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: Repairing the focal opening first targets a finding whose manipulation does not reproduce or relieve the complaint. It is not the supported initial treatment for this broad functional symptom.

answerChoices.label: Plicate the broad midline; then start core rehabilitation at follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: Plication may be discussed for selected persistent functional symptoms, but no conservative treatment has been tried and the intact broad midline is not an acute defect requiring reconstruction.

decisionNodes.explanation: There are two findings: a broad intact but separated midline and a focal reducible opening. The weakness follows the broad segment, not the focal protrusion. Consider rehabilitation first and observe the asymptomatic focal defect. If symptoms instead localized to that opening and improved with reduction, the focal repair pathway would become more appropriate.

cases.presentation: {patientName}, a 60-year-old man, attends clinic after discharge while the founder reviews an outside emergency ventral-hernia operation. The trapped bowel regained perfusion after release. During adhesiolysis a full-thickness small-bowel enterotomy was recognized immediately and securely repaired. A limited local spill was removed; repeated inspection found no continuing leak, residual contamination or bowel segment needing reassessment. He was off vasoactive support before and after this event, with maintained perfusion and no ongoing resuscitation requirement. The fascia met with gentle approximation and a closed tissue layer separated bowel from the available reinforcement plane.

decisionNodes.stem: Which reinforcement strategy best fits {patientName}'s recorded end-of-operation findings?

answerChoices.label: Complete repair with permanent macroporous synthetic reinforcement
answerChoices.rationale: The recognized repaired injury, source-controlled field, recovered bowel, stable physiology and directly closable wall fit the selected emergency repair scope. When mesh reinforcement is chosen in that scope, current guidance favors permanent macroporous synthetic material.

answerChoices.label: Complete repair with non-cross-linked porcine dermal reinforcement
answerChoices.rationale: A biologic material is not preferentially required by a controlled enterotomy in an otherwise eligible repair. Current guidance favors permanent macroporous synthetic mesh in this selected scope.

answerChoices.label: Defer reinforcement and use temporary abdominal coverage
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied observations establish direct closure feasibility and no remaining source-control, bowel reassessment or physiological indication for temporary coverage.

decisionNodes.explanation: The bowel event is explicitly a repaired enterotomy during adhesiolysis, not an unexplained opening. decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan best fits {patientName}'s current fluid-pocket course and the newly posted culture result?

answerChoices.label: Continue observation with a clinic reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The shrinking painless simple pocket and healed noninflamed wound support observation. The earlier surface swab does not establish a deep organism in an unsampled pocket or a current clinical skin infection.

answerChoices.label: Perform sterile image-guided aspiration with culture
answerChoices.rationale: An improving asymptomatic pocket does not need aspiration merely to chase a surface-swab result. Puncture carries an inoculation concern; new symptoms or deep-infection evidence would change that balance.

answerChoices.label: Start oral cephalexin with a clinic reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Cephalexin is a credible susceptible-staphylococcal skin-infection medicine, but there is no current inflamed wound or supported deep bacterial infection to treat. A positive prior surface swab is not itself an indication.

answerChoices.rationale: The lesion was removed intact in one resection; later laboratory division does not make that procedure piecemeal. Size establishes an advanced adenoma with confident complete removal.

decisionNodes.stem: Which referral should guide {patientName}'s next treatment plan?

answerChoices.label: Advanced-endoscopy referral for completion-resection planning
answerChoices.rationale: Prior cautery and tattoo beneath the residual lesion can produce fibrosis. Expert completion planning is warranted; nonlifting alone does not prove deep invasion.

answerChoices.label: Colorectal-surgery referral for oncologic resection planning
answerChoices.rationale: This lift test was performed after interventions that can scar the submucosa; the original granular morphology and lack of an invasive focus matter.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic-endoscopy referral for repeat biopsy planning
answerChoices.rationale: Another limited sample may miss invasion and does not solve the scarred completion-resection problem.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret a lift test in its procedural history. Tattoo and cautery beneath a residual lesion can cause fibrosis, so this nonlift does not independently establish deep invasion. Advanced completion-resection planning addresses the actual problem without assuming either cancer or easy routine snare removal.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Biopsy confirms sigmoid adenocarcinoma and distant staging is negative. decisionNodes.stem: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded anatomy, subject to confirmation of clear margins at surgery?

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc partial cystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A focal dome attachment can be removed en bloc with a bladder portion while retaining uninvolved neck, trigone and reservoir; the plan still requires an achievable clear margin.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc total cystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented attachment is focal at the dome; the record does not show neck/trigone involvement or loss of a usable remaining bladder requiring total removal.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with separation of the bladder attachment
answerChoices.rationale: An adherent cancer interface should not be divided to decide whether the adhesion is malignant; partial bladder resection preserves an en-bloc specimen.

decisionNodes.explanation: First preserve the adherent tumor-organ interface. Adherence does not itself establish histologic invasion, and total cystectomy is not automatic.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s current metastatic-primary record?

answerChoices.label: Systemic treatment planning with the primary left in place
answerChoices.rationale: The record lacks clinical or radiographic obstruction and other primary-related complications. For incurable metastatic disease in this setting, systemic treatment generally precedes prophylactic primary surgery.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy followed by systemic treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: The smaller scope passed, bowel function continues and CT shows no upstream dilation; prophylactic colectomy would delay treatment of the dominant metastatic disease.

decisionNodes.explanation: The adult scope's nonpassage does not alone establish bowel obstruction. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The founder reviews the operative decision recorded during his outside admission for a perforated sigmoid primary with unresectable liver and lung metastases. Before admission he requested treatment of reversible acute complications. At the recorded decision point, the perforated sigmoid segment had been resected and the remaining bowel ends were viable. Diffuse fecal contamination had been encountered. Despite fluids, antibiotics and resection, norepinephrine was still required and the bowel was edematous. The operative team judged fascial closure feasible without a planned open abdomen.
decisionNodes.stem: At that outside intraoperative decision point, which reconstruction plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded findings?

answerChoices.label: Close the rectal stump and create an end colostomy
answerChoices.rationale: Ongoing vasopressor need with fecal contamination and edematous bowel favors avoiding a new colorectal anastomosis. A concrete Hartmann reconstruction is supported here; no universal rule for every perforation is asserted.

answerChoices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis and a diverting loop ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: Diversion does not remove an anastomosis or its failure risk. The continuing vasopressor need and adverse local conditions favor not constructing it at this recorded point.

answerChoices.label: Create a colorectal anastomosis without proximal diversion
answerChoices.rationale: The relevant observations are the current vasopressor need, contamination and edema, not earlier cancer-treatment eligibility.

decisionNodes.explanation: Review the physiology at the actual reconstruction point. Persistent vasopressor need plus fecal contamination and bowel edema favor avoiding a colorectal anastomosis; closing the stump and forming an end colostomy is a concrete plan. Diversion cannot erase the risk of an anastomosis already constructed. This scoped decision does not prescribe Hartmann reconstruction for every perforated cancer.

decisionNodes.stem: Which current management plan best fits {patientName}’s postoperative incision-site collection?

answerChoices.label: Clinical observation with reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The current functional course differs from the earlier symptomatic episode. Reappearance or a modest imaging increase does not by itself establish a need for another invasive procedure in this uncomplicated pocket.

answerChoices.label: Repeat image-guided needle aspiration
answerChoices.rationale: Aspiration helped the earlier painful pocket, but the present functional limitation has resolved. Repeating it solely because the image is larger adds a procedure without the former indication.

answerChoices.rationale: This is a real option for selected difficult recurrent collections, but one recurrence with recovered function is not evidence that a drain is now needed.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret recurrence and current effect separately. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A prior obstetric ultrasound showed an anterior sphincter defect. With formed stools she can defer defecation and retain stool during activity. Her diary records accidents after sudden urges on days with loose stool. A completed continence-focused rehabilitation course improved voluntary squeeze but not those loose-stool episodes. Psyllium caused persistent bloating and was stopped. Assessment found no fecal loading or infectious or inflammatory cause of the chronic loose stool.
decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment should {patientName} try next for this remaining leakage pattern?

answerChoices.label: Continence biofeedback
answerChoices.rationale: Biofeedback is a genuine continence treatment. Here a completed course improved squeeze while the residual accidents remained tied to loose stools, making stool-directed medication the more useful next trial.

answerChoices.label: Overlapping sphincteroplasty
answerChoices.rationale: A defect can inform repair planning, but the ability to retain formed stool and the current treatment-response pattern argue for addressing stool consistency before proceeding from anatomy to reconstruction.

answerChoices.label: Loperamide therapy
answerChoices.rationale: The residual problem tracks loose-stool urgency despite retained formed-stool control and improved squeeze. A monitored stool-firming medicine is a reasonable next conservative trial after poorly tolerated bulking; the old defect does not by itself require reconstruction.

decisionNodes.explanation: Compare what improved with what still causes accidents. Voluntary squeeze improved and formed stools are retained, whereas loose-stool urgency remains. A monitored loperamide trial targets that residual contributor before an operation based on the old defect; continence biofeedback is not being characterized as evacuation training.

answerChoices.rationale: Current functional relaxation argues against residual nonrelaxing puborectalis as the treatment target. Injection does not correct the retaining pouch.

answerChoices.rationale: STARR is not recommended for rectocele or internal intussusception because of its complication profile. A relevant anatomical target does not validate every operation directed at it.

decisionNodes.stem: Using the outside hospital's stated worksheet, which starting infusion rate should have been recorded for {patientName} at arrival, rounded to the nearest whole mL/hour?

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 378 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: Count 14% plus 8%, giving 22%. The first allocation is 3 × 70 × 22 / 2 = 2310 mL. Subtract 800 mL, then divide the remaining 1510 mL by the four hours remaining: 377.5 mL/hour.

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 693 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: This result counts the additional epidermal erythema: (3 × 70 × 34 / 2 − 800) / 4 = 692.5. The intact red region does not belong in this dermal-burn estimate.

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 189 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: This result restarts an eight-hour window at arrival: (2310 − 800) / 8 = 188.75. The supplied worksheet measures time from the injury.

decisionNodes.explanation: The dermal-burn total is 22%, not the 34% of visibly changed skin. The worksheet's first allocation is 2310 mL; 1510 mL remains after transport fluid. Four hours remain in its injury-based window, giving 377.5, rounded to 378 mL/hour. This calculation applies only to the specified worksheet.

answerChoices.rationale: This is a genuine cyanide regimen, but sodium nitrite can worsen hypotension and oxygen carriage through methemoglobin formation when CO poisoning coexists. The preferred available alternative here is hydroxocobalamin.

answerChoices.label: Await the blood cyanide result before antidote treatment
answerChoices.rationale: A reference-laboratory result should not defer treatment when severe exposure and clinical findings make suspicion high.

decisionNodes.explanation: Infer possible cyanide toxicity in addition to the measured CO exposure, then account for the oxygen-carriage and hypotension risks of sodium nitrite when choosing treatment. decisionNodes.stem: Which next procedure best fits {patientName}'s acquired ventilatory findings in the later burn-unit record?

answerChoices.label: Flexible bronchoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: The isolated peak-pressure rise favors resistance. A passable positioned tube, retained particulate secretions and new lobar volume loss point beyond the tube to lower-airway material that bronchoscopy can inspect and remove.

answerChoices.rationale: The tube has a documented passable lumen and appropriate position. Those observations make a primary tube problem less compelling than retained material beyond it.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: On admission, intermittent cramps had become continuous with repeated retching. His abdomen was tender without guarding; pulse was 96/min and blood pressure 122/76 mmHg. The record showed normal renal function and no prior contrast reaction.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial study best fits {patientName}'s recorded acute presentation after gastric bypass?

answerChoices.label: Upper endoscopy of the pouch and anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: Endoscopy assesses the pouch and gastrojejunal lumen, but it does not survey the entire altered mesenteric and intestinal anatomy needed for this acute pain course.

answerChoices.label: Computed tomography with oral and intravenous contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Contrast-enhanced CT surveys the altered bowel limbs, mesentery and possible extraluminal complications in this stable acute presentation.

answerChoices.label: Water-soluble contrast examination of the upper gastrointestinal tract
answerChoices.rationale: A luminal contrast study can assess proximal passage or leakage, but it provides less complete evaluation of the bowel and mesentery for the current acute course.

decisionNodes.explanation: The change to persistent acute pain after RYGB requires assessment beyond the pouch lumen. Contrast-enhanced CT with oral contrast evaluates the reconstructed bowel pathways and extraluminal anatomy. This is a review of the hospital investigation, not a clinic CT order.
sourceLabels: World Society of Emergency Surgery / IFSO; World Journal of Emergency Surgery (2022)

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: CT was acquired with oral and intravenous contrast and reviewed with the bypass operative report. It showed no fixed transition, no free air and no reported mesenteric swirl. Despite fluids and repeated reassessment, continuous pain and retching persisted and focal tenderness increased. Lactate remained within that laboratory's interval.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next hospital action best fits {patientName}'s continuing course after the CT?

answerChoices.label: Repeat contrast CT after another observation period
answerChoices.rationale: The first study was adequately acquired for the question. Another observation-and-scan cycle does not resolve the concerning persistent course and can delay recognition of an internal hernia.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Endoscopy is useful for a luminal source, but persistent acute symptoms after RYGB can arise from an internal hernia outside its field. The negative CT and normal lactate do not settle that risk.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to diagnostic surgical laparoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent acute pain and retching with increasing tenderness after RYGB justify prompt exploration despite inconclusive CT. A normal lactate is not evidence that the concerning course has resolved.

decisionNodes.explanation: A negative CT does not exclude an internal hernia after RYGB. The persistent acute symptoms and increasing tenderness justify prompt surgical exploration in the recorded hospital setting. Neither a normal lactate nor the absence of a reported swirl substitutes for clinical reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Begin nirogacestat through sarcoma oncology

answerChoices.label: Deliver external-beam radiotherapy to the mesenteric tumor

answerChoices.label: Continue the existing clinical/MRI surveillance plan

answerChoices.rationale: Aspiration is a reasonable intervention when conservative management is unsuitable. The initial pain improved and the remaining rim alone does not establish that need under BTS.

answerChoices.rationale: The record does not show persisting substantial symptoms, physiological compromise or a failed less invasive plan requiring a drain.

decisionNodes.explanation: At the decision time, {patientName} has minimal pain, no breathlessness and stable observations after analgesia. Under the specified BTS approach, conservative management can be considered in a suitable minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax irrespective of size. The unchanged 3 cm rim does not by itself overturn that assessment. Aspiration or chest drainage may be appropriate when conservative management is unsuitable; the earlier pain does not prove that it remains unsuitable after reassessment. Follow-up, return advice and patient choice still matter.

answerChoices.label: Tunneled indwelling pleural catheter placement
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated symptomatic benefit identifies a useful drainage target; persistent nonapposition makes an IPC preferable to attempting talc pleurodesis.

answerChoices.label: Chest-tube talc slurry pleurodesis
answerChoices.rationale: Talc depends on adequate pleural apposition. Persistent broad separation with a visceral rind makes successful apposition unlikely in this record.

answerChoices.label: Repeat therapeutic thoracentesis when symptomatic
answerChoices.rationale: This can palliate symptoms, but repeated rapid reaccumulation has already required two procedures. An accepted definitive drainage option is preferable in this ongoing-care context.

decisionNodes.explanation: {patientName} repeatedly breathes better after fluid removal, so this effusion is a meaningful symptom target. The persistent large pleural separation, patent central bronchi and visceral rind together support nonexpandable lung; the air-fluid space alone would not establish that conclusion. An IPC can provide ongoing drainage without requiring the apposition needed for talc pleurodesis. Repeat aspiration remains a patient-specific option, but the two episodes of rapid symptomatic recurrence and feasible catheter care favor IPC among these plans. The choice requires discussion of burden and goals; it is not a universal rule based on cytology alone.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial mediastinal investigation best fits {patientName} before the proposed lung operation?

answerChoices.label: Systematic EBUS/EUS-guided nodal sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The enlarged FDG-avid node requires tissue assessment, and endosonographic sampling is the preferred initial invasive route when available.

answerChoices.label: Cervical mediastinoscopy with nodal sampling
answerChoices.rationale: This can obtain nodal tissue but is more invasive than the recommended initial endosonographic approach for an accessible paratracheal target.

answerChoices.label: Repeat FDG-PET/CT after infection recovery
answerChoices.rationale: Inflammation can explain uptake, but repeating metabolic imaging does not establish the tissue stage of this enlarged suspicious mediastinal node before surgery.

decisionNodes.explanation: FDG uptake during recovery from infection cannot prove nodal metastasis, but it also cannot safely dismiss an enlarged node that may change the operative plan. Tissue staging is needed. Systematic endosonographic sampling is the preferred initial invasive approach for accessible mediastinal nodes. Mediastinoscopy can obtain tissue but does not need to precede an available appropriate endosonographic approach. Repeating PET cannot supply histology. The next step after a negative sample depends on adequacy, residual suspicion and the applicable current guideline; this item does not impose a universal rule for that later decision.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next diagnostic plan best fits {patientName}'s serial nodule findings and access anatomy?

answerChoices.label: Navigational bronchoscopy with nodule sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The serial CT change remains concerning despite nonavid PET. A bronchus entering the lesion supports a bronchoscopic route, while bullae make the percutaneous paths less attractive.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided percutaneous nodule core biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Tissue investigation is appropriate, but the available needle paths cross bullous emphysema and carry greater pneumothorax concern than the available airway route.

answerChoices.label: Short-interval diagnostic chest CT surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Nonavid PET does not erase the substantial dimensional increase on comparable scans over the stated interval. Continued imaging alone leaves that concerning trajectory unresolved.

decisionNodes.explanation: The dated matched CT studies show a substantial size increase over nine months. A nonavid PET cannot establish benignity of that lesion. Further diagnostic investigation is therefore appropriate among these choices. A bronchus entering the nodule supports bronchoscopic sampling, with navigation used to aid access; bullous emphysema on the available transthoracic paths increases pneumothorax concern. Those findings favor the offered bronchoscopic plan over reflexive percutaneous sampling. Route selection still depends on local expertise and individual anatomy, and is not a universal rule for all peripheral nodules.

decisionNodes.stem: Under the SEOM thymic-tumour guideline, which procedural plan best fits {patientName}'s current work-up?

answerChoices.label: Complete thymectomy with intact lesion removal
answerChoices.rationale: The pattern favors a localized resectable thymic epithelial lesion. Complete thymectomy includes the lesion and remaining thymus rather than limited mass excision.

answerChoices.label: Limited lesion excision with thymus preservation
answerChoices.rationale: This is a distinct operation, but the specified guideline prefers complete thymectomy for the suspected resectable thymic epithelial tumour scenario.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous core biopsy before treatment selection
answerChoices.rationale: Biopsy is appropriate when histology is needed to choose treatment, but it is not mandatory for a highly probable completely resectable thymic epithelial lesion.

decisionNodes.explanation: The solid enhancing thymic-bed lesion, preserved tissue planes and lack of separate nodal or pleural disease favor a localized resectable thymic epithelial tumour. These observations do not prove histology, and normal AFP and beta-hCG do not exclude all alternatives. decisionNodes.stem: Which additional treatment backbone best fits {patientName}'s current graft findings after the completed steroid course?

answerChoices.label: Rabbit antithymocyte globulin therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Failure to improve after steroids is not by itself evidence of refractory cellular rejection; the current distribution and antibodies point to a humoral process.

answerChoices.label: Plasma exchange with intravenous immunoglobulin
answerChoices.rationale: The microvascular, complement and donor-specific antibody findings support an acute active humoral process for which this is a consensus backbone, with limited comparative efficacy evidence.

answerChoices.label: Stepwise reduction of maintenance immunosuppression
answerChoices.rationale: Reduction is important for BK disease in the appropriate context, but the represented viral assessment is negative and the microvascular antibody findings require a different strategy.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the new specimen before treating steroid nonresponse as cellular rescue failure. Capillary inflammation, C4d and donor-specific antibodies support an active antibody-mediated process; the represented tissue lacks a cellular component and chronic glomerular remodeling. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The outside record concerns a deceased-donor kidney transplant. Dialysis was needed after implantation. A core on postoperative day 3 showed acute tubular injury without rejection. It is now postoperative day 11: urine output remains low, creatinine has not fallen between dialysis sessions, and dialysis is still required. No fever or new infectious symptoms are documented. Supportive care continues with each proposed plan.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next graft-assessment plan best fits {patientName}'s postoperative course through day 11?

answerChoices.label: Repeat kidney-allograft core tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The earlier sample establishes what was present then; continuing delayed function warrants reassessment for a new or previously unrepresented parenchymal process.

answerChoices.label: Continue supportive care with graft-function monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Supportive care remains necessary, but an old tubular-injury sample does not establish the current cause of persistent nonrecovery.

answerChoices.label: Give intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Continuing delayed function does not establish rejection, and the cause can be assessed with tissue before directing antirejection therapy.

decisionNodes.explanation: The day-3 core is evidence about that time point. By day 11 there is still no functional recovery, so its tubular-injury finding should not substitute for current parenchymal assessment. KDIGO suggests interval biopsies during delayed function, albeit with low-quality evidence; the constructed chronology illustrates that reassessment rather than establishing a universal biopsy day. answerChoices.label: Upfront gastrectomy, then postoperative chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a pre-initial-treatment cytology result as if it were a finding discovered during an already undertaken gastrectomy. The chronology matters.

decisionNodes.stem: Which postoperative treatment should be discussed for {patientName}'s gastric cancer on the basis of the outside operative and pathology records?

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Capecitabine and oxaliplatin are supported after curative D2 surgery for stage II/III disease. This is postoperative treatment after upfront surgery, not selection of a new perioperative regimen.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant capecitabine chemoradiation
answerChoices.rationale: The completed R0 D2 record lacks the margin or inadequate-dissection boundary that would make a postoperative local-control strategy more compelling.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX plus nivolumab
answerChoices.rationale: The adjuvant nivolumab trial after upfront D2 surgery did not establish added benefit. A newer perioperative immunotherapy approval is not interchangeable with this postoperative-only plan.

decisionNodes.explanation: Match systemic treatment to the pathway that actually occurred. Stage III disease after upfront R0 D2 resection supports adjuvant CAPOX among these options. Adequate dissection and clear margins affect the radiation comparison; postoperative nivolumab is not established by perioperative immunotherapy results.

decisionNodes.stem: Which operation best fits {patientName}'s localized gastric tumor?

answerChoices.label: Full-thickness wedge gastrectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A limited resection can remove this peripheral conventional GIST with an intact capsule. Its lymphatic behavior differs from gastric adenocarcinoma, so routine D2 clearance is not required.

answerChoices.label: Total gastrectomy with D2 dissection
answerChoices.rationale: This applies an epithelial gastric-cancer operation and routine nodal strategy to a fundic mesenchymal tumor, with more gastric loss and no stated nodal indication.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic submucosal enucleation
answerChoices.rationale: Shelling out a muscular-wall GIST does not provide the same assurance of complete excision with an intact capsule and appropriate wall clearance.

decisionNodes.explanation: The biopsy establishes a conventional GIST pattern, and the peripheral fundic anatomy permits a local full-thickness excision. Preserve the capsule and obtain complete removal; do not substitute routine adenocarcinoma lymphadenectomy or shelling out the mass.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next management plan best fits {patientName}'s returned gastric-GIST resection records?

answerChoices.label: Scheduled CT tumor surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A microscopic margin does not equal rupture or macroscopic residual tumor. Given the limited tumor risk features and major completion operation, review-based surveillance is the best offered plan rather than automatic resection or imatinib for the margin itself.

answerChoices.label: Completion total gastrectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The microscopic edge does not by itself establish benefit sufficient to justify the represented major gastric loss. Low-morbidity re-excision is a different discussion.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant imatinib treatment
answerChoices.rationale: R1 status alone is not an adjuvant-imatinib criterion. The reported size, gastric site, low mitotic count and absence of rupture do not supply a high-risk indication in this case.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read margin, gross residual tumor and rupture as separate findings. A microscopic edge in an otherwise intact, macroscopically complete resection does not independently require major completion surgery or adjuvant imatinib. The actual re-excision burden and tumor risk support surveillance among these choices.

decisionNodes.stem: Which postoperative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s completely resected gastric tumor?

answerChoices.label: CT surveillance after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: The adverse risk features justify close sarcoma follow-up, but do not make an imatinib-resistant driver sensitive. Metastatic avapritinib activity does not establish routine adjuvant benefit after complete resection.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant imatinib after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: Size and mitotic activity cannot overcome primary D842V resistance. Adjuvant imatinib is not indicated for this molecular subtype.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant avapritinib after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: Selecting an active drug from the metastatic setting does not establish an adjuvant indication in a patient with complete local removal. A clinical trial is a separate discussion.

decisionNodes.explanation: High recurrence risk is not a substitute for a supported adjuvant drug. D842V excludes routine adjuvant imatinib, and the established avapritinib indication concerns unresectable or metastatic disease. Use risk-based surveillance and sarcoma review rather than invent an adjuvant standard.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial tumor-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s gastric-mass records?

answerChoices.label: Preoperative imatinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The genotype supports imatinib responsiveness, and the anatomy gives shrinkage a consequential operative purpose. The combination supports a neoadjuvant plan rather than treatment from size alone.

answerChoices.label: Primary gastrectomy with margin-negative resection
answerChoices.rationale: Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative avapritinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The molecular result and operative cost must both matter. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib responsiveness, while the cardia involvement gives response a reason to precede resection. Reassess the operation after treatment rather than assuming that every large GIST or every kinase inhibitor has the same pathway.

answerChoices.rationale: A contaminated puncture with an unestablished primary series requires active and passive protection; a single remembered shot does not document the series.

answerChoices.label: Tetanus-containing vaccine; no TIG
answerChoices.rationale: Vaccine alone does not provide the indicated passive protection for this dirty wound with an unknown series.

answerChoices.label: TIG; no tetanus-containing vaccine
answerChoices.rationale: TIG supplies temporary antibody but does not replace the needed active immunization in an unestablished series.

answerChoices.label: Neither tetanus-containing vaccine nor TIG
answerChoices.rationale: The actual record does not establish the completed recent series needed for that conclusion.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use the documented series status. One recalled injection is not proof of a completed primary series. The soil-contaminated puncture therefore calls for both vaccine and TIG at the reviewed encounter; no product dose or catch-up schedule is prescribed here.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next diagnostic step best addresses {patientName}'s persistent enlarging nodule?

answerChoices.label: Obtain a new incisional specimen for histology
answerChoices.rationale: The acquisition did not include tissue needed to assess the palpable lesion. A new adequate sample addresses that limitation; appearance does not establish its diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: Request additional sections from the current specimen
answerChoices.rationale: Additional levels cannot add anatomical tissue that was not acquired. Only superficial material was submitted while the palpable lesion remains.

answerChoices.label: Request specialist review of the current specimen
answerChoices.rationale: Expert review can clarify interpretation, but cannot identify deeper lesional tissue absent from the material.

decisionNodes.explanation: The sampled location was correct; its depth was not adequate for the remaining nodule. Distinguish missing tissue from a need for more sections or another interpretation. Obtain an adequate deeper biopsy before scar-directed treatment. This does not diagnose a particular malignancy.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next step was warranted by the recorded change in {patientName}'s flap?

answerChoices.label: Proceed to urgent microsurgical pedicle exploration
answerChoices.rationale: Combined flap findings suggest threatened local outflow despite persistent inflow and native perfusion. Assess a correctable pedicle problem before nonoperative salvage.

answerChoices.label: Obtain native-limb arterial angiography before exploration
answerChoices.rationale: The leading concern is localized to the flap while native perfusion remains present. This makes another study a prerequisite for exploration of a potentially correctable flap problem.

answerChoices.label: Start medicinal-leech offloading before exploration
answerChoices.rationale: Offloading does not correct a mechanical pedicle problem. A surgically remediable cause remains unassessed.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use skin findings and ipsilateral circulation together: a tense violaceous paddle with brisk dark bleeding suggests threatened flap outflow. Urgent microsurgical exploration addresses a potentially remediable pedicle problem. An arterial sound does not guarantee tissue perfusion, and leeches do not repair an obstructed pedicle.

decisionNodes.stem: Which rescue drainage procedure should the referral team discuss for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: After failed ERCP, expert EUS-guided drainage is favored when anatomy and local experience support it.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: This is an important alternative, but current BSG guidance favors expert EUS drainage after failed distal-obstruction ERCP when feasible.

answerChoices.label: Operative bypass with hepaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: A surgical bypass is more invasive than the expert rescue approaches available for this stable patient.

decisionNodes.stem: Which interim drainage procedure should the consulting HPB team arrange for {patientName} before definitive repair?

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The septic proximal ducts remain obstructed despite collection drainage, and the retrograde route cannot traverse the injury. Transhepatic drainage accesses the proximal system.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: This assumes an accessible path into the obstructed proximal ducts that the attributed injection and wire attempt did not establish.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous exchange of the collection catheter
answerChoices.rationale: The collection is already collapsed; changing its catheter does not decompress the dilated proximal duct system.

decisionNodes.explanation: The studies distinguish a controlled extrabiliary cavity from an obstructed proximal duct system. Infection persists while the papillary route cannot reach that system. Transhepatic biliary drainage is a supported interim decompression option under HPB management; no repair date or universal reconstruction is selected.
